fields.title: The Key Teachings of Martin Luther
fields.subtitle: An Ochorus companion to his life and teaching
fields.description: A concise, faithful guide to the heart of Martin Luther’s teaching — the righteousness of God given as a gift, faith alone, the theology of the cross, law and gospel, the freedom of a Christian, the Word, vocation, prayer and comfort for the dying — told honestly, with his grave faults named. Twenty short chapters, each ending in questions and a prayer, written by Ochorus as a companion to Luther’s own public-domain works, which readers are warmly encouraged to go to directly.
fields.about_html:
This is not a book by Martin Luther. It is a companion to him — an independent work of exposition and appreciation, written by Ochorus, that gathers the heart of his teaching into twenty short chapters for the ordinary reader, with an account of his life, a conclusion, and a guide to his writings. It draws its quotations only from the six of his sermons that sit in the Ochorus library; his treatises, catechisms and commentaries are described in the present author’s own words.

Luther’s teaching has one thread. The righteousness God requires is the righteousness God gives, freely, in Christ, and it is received by faith alone; and everything he wrote about the cross, the law, the will, the Word, the sacraments, prayer, work, marriage and death is that discovery followed out into the whole of life. This volume follows the thread, and it is plain about the places where Luther must be read with sorrow as well as gratitude — above all his late writings against the Jews, his savage words in the Peasants’ War, and the coarseness of his polemic.

Luther’s own writings are in the public domain and freely available in older English translations, and every chapter here names the work it draws on so that the reader can go to the source. This companion is offered only to open the door. Scripture is quoted from the Authorised (King James) Version, and nothing here claims to stand in for the man’s own vigorous, earthy and consoling pages.

fields.title: Introduction
fields.body_html:
For therein is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith: as it is written, The just shall live by faith. ROMANS 1:17

Few people have changed the world as much as Martin Luther, and few have been so often claimed, so often blamed, and so seldom read. He was a German friar and professor of the Bible who set out, in the autumn of 1517, to start an academic argument about indulgences, and ended by dividing the Western church. Statues of him stand in German squares. Churches around the world bear his name. Historians argue over what he caused and what he did not. And yet the heart of what he taught is not complicated at all. It is the discovery of a frightened man that God is not against him but for him, and that the righteousness he could never manufacture had been given to him as a gift.

He was born in 1483 at Eisleben in Saxony, the son of a miner who had worked his way up into the copper trade and wanted his clever boy to be a lawyer. He became instead an Augustinian friar, a priest, a doctor of theology and a lecturer on the Psalms and the letters of Paul at the small new university of Wittenberg. From that lecture-room came the Reformation. He died in 1546, in the town where he was born, having translated the Bible into German, written hymns that are still sung, taught a nation to pray its catechism, married a runaway nun, raised a family and preached some thousands of sermons.

Why he still matters

Luther matters because he asked the question every awakened conscience asks — how can I stand before a holy God? — and he refused every answer but the one Scripture gives. He had tried the other answers. He had fasted, confessed, watched and prayed as few monks did, and they had left him more afraid than before. When at last he saw in Paul that the righteousness of God is not only the justice by which God judges but the gift by which He justifies, he said that it was as if the gates of heaven had opened. Every Protestant church, and a great deal of modern Catholic teaching too, has had to reckon with that moment.

He matters also because he gave the gospel back to ordinary people. He believed the ploughboy and the housewife should hear God speak in their own tongue, pray in their own words, sing in their own church, and serve God in their own kitchen and field without apology. The German Bible, the congregational hymn, the household catechism and the dignity of daily work are all, in part, his gifts.

The one thread

If there is one thread that runs through everything Luther taught, it is two small words: for you. The gospel is not simply the story of what Christ did; it is the announcement that He did it for me. Luther makes the point again and again in his sermons. Preaching on the angel’s message to the shepherds, he asks:

“Of what benefit would it be to me if Christ had been born a thousand times … if I were never to hear that he was born for me and was to be my very own?”

That is the whole of Luther in a sentence. Faith is not agreeing that the history is true, for the devils do that. Faith is laying hold of Christ as mine: His righteousness mine, His death mine, His life mine. Out of that grows everything else — the joy, the freedom, the love of neighbour, the courage in death.

Unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given. ISAIAH 9:6

How this book is arranged

The second chapter tells his life. The twenty chapters that follow each take one of his key teachings, beginning where he began, with the righteousness of God in Romans, and ending where every life ends, with his comfort for the dying. Between them come faith alone, the theology of the cross, law and gospel, the freedom of a Christian, the bondage of the will, the Word, the priesthood of all believers, vocation, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, prayer, the catechism, spiritual struggle, music, marriage, the two kingdoms, the devil, and the believer who is righteous and a sinner at once.

Ochorus hosts six of Luther’s sermons, in an older English translation: on the birth of Jesus, on the appearing of the grace of God, on Christ’s sufferings, on His resurrection, on the office of the Holy Spirit, and on Paul’s praise of love. Wherever Luther is quoted in these pages, it is from those sermons. His great treatises — The Freedom of a Christian, The Bondage of the Will, the catechisms, the lectures on Galatians and the rest — are described in the present author’s own words, and a guide to them is given at the end.

Each chapter ends with application points and a prayer. Luther would have approved. He thought theology that did not end in prayer and comfort was not worth the ink, and he wrote his little book on prayer for his barber.

Reading him with care

This is not a book of hero-worship, and Luther would have mocked one. He knew himself to be a sinner, and he said so loudly. But his readers must go further than he did, because some of his sins were public, written and deadly.

Three things must be named plainly at the outset. First, and gravest, in his last years he wrote against the Jews with a hatred that cannot be excused. In On the Jews and Their Lies, published in 1543, he urged that synagogues be burned, Jewish homes destroyed and Jewish teachers silenced. Twenty years earlier he had written kindly of them, hoping they would come to Christ; when they did not, he turned savage. Those pages were revived and used by the Nazis in the twentieth century, and many Lutheran churches have since formally repudiated them. No appreciation of Luther is honest that passes over this. Second, in the Peasants’ War of 1525 he urged the princes to strike down the rebels without mercy, in language that still shocks. Third, his polemic against opponents — popes, fellow Reformers, Anabaptists — was often coarse, abusive and unjust, and it helped to harden divisions that have lasted five centuries.

Prove all things; hold fast that which is good. 1 THESSALONIANS 5:21

None of this cancels what he saw in Romans. But it is a warning, and Luther’s own teaching explains it: a man can be justified by faith and still be a sinner, and a great teacher of grace can be terribly wrong. We read him, then, as he told us to read everyone — under the Word of God, holding fast what agrees with it and letting go what does not. What agrees with it, on grace, faith, the cross and the comfort of the gospel, is some of the richest treasure the church possesses.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Ask yourself honestly: do I believe that Christ did what He did for me, by name? Write the words “for me” beside a verse such as Galatians 2:20 and pray over it.

2. Name the answers you have tried, other than Christ, to the question of how you can stand before God. Bring them to Him and lay them down.

3. If you know Luther only as a statue or a slogan, resolve to read one of his sermons in the Ochorus library this week.

4. Consider how you speak of those you disagree with. Luther’s worst sins began with his tongue and his pen. Ask God to guard yours.

5. Set aside a regular time to read one chapter of this book slowly, and to pray at the end of it.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You have not waited for me to become righteous before You would love me; You have given me the righteousness of Your Son as a gift.
Teach me to hear the gospel as good news for me, and not only as a story about others.
Keep me honest about the sins of those I admire, and more honest still about my own.
And as I read of Your servant Martin, let me find not him but You, the God who justifies the ungodly, through Jesus Christ our Lord. Amen.

fields.title: Thunder, a Cloister and a Door in Wittenberg
fields.body_html:
I will cry unto God most high; unto God that performeth all things for me. PSALM 57:2

A miner’s son. Martin Luther was born on 10 November 1483 at Eisleben, in the county of Mansfeld in Saxony, and baptised the next day, the feast of St Martin, whose name he was given. His father, Hans, came of peasant stock and had gone into the copper mines; by hard work he rose to lease smelters of his own and to sit on the town council of Mansfeld, where the family soon moved. His mother, Margarethe, was a devout and hard-working woman. The home was strict, the schooling stricter, and the boy learned early both the fear of punishment and the fear of God. He was sent to school at Mansfeld, then at Magdeburg and Eisenach, and in 1501 to the University of Erfurt, where he took his master’s degree in 1505. His father had chosen his career: he was to study law.

The storm. He did not study it for long. On 2 July 1505, walking back to Erfurt after a visit home, he was caught in a violent thunderstorm near the village of Stotternheim. Lightning struck close beside him and threw him to the ground. In terror he cried out to St Anne, the patron of miners, vowing to become a monk. A fortnight later, against his father’s furious opposition, he entered the house of the Augustinian friars at Erfurt. He was ordained priest in 1507.

The anxious friar. He was, by every account, an exemplary monk: he prayed the hours, fasted, kept vigils and confessed with painful thoroughness. But none of it brought peace. The more he strove, the more he saw that God requires not only outward acts but a pure heart and a perfect love, and he knew he did not have them. He feared God’s righteousness as a sword. His superior and confessor, Johann von Staupitz, a gentle and wise man, pointed him to the wounds of Christ and, to occupy his troubled mind, set him to study for a doctorate. In 1510 Luther went to Rome on the business of his order and was shaken by the worldliness he saw. In 1512 he became a doctor of theology and took up the chair of Bible at the young University of Wittenberg, in Electoral Saxony, which he was to hold for the rest of his life.

The gate of paradise. There, lecturing on the Psalms, then on Romans, Galatians and Hebrews, he wrestled with Paul’s words in Romans 1:17. He had been taught to read the righteousness of God as the justice by which God punishes the unrighteous, and he confessed later that he had come to hate that word. Then, pondering the whole verse, he saw that it speaks of the righteousness by which God, in mercy, makes the sinner righteous through faith: the just shall live by faith. It was, he said long afterwards, as though he had been born again and had gone through open gates into paradise. Scholars still argue about exactly when this happened; what matters is that it happened, and that it changed everything.

Ninety-five theses. In 1517 the Dominican preacher Johann Tetzel was selling indulgences near Wittenberg, promising remission of the punishment of sins, even for the dead, to raise money for the rebuilding of St Peter’s in Rome. Luther’s own people went to buy them. On 31 October he sent ninety-five theses for debate to the Archbishop of Mainz, and by long tradition he posted them on the door of the Castle Church. Whether the nailing happened is debated; that the theses were soon printed and read across Germany is not. What began as an academic protest became a public storm.

The break. The next four years moved quickly. In 1518 he explained his theology of the cross to his own order at Heidelberg and was questioned by a papal legate at Augsburg. In 1519, debating with Johann Eck at Leipzig, he was driven to say that popes and councils could err. In 1520 he published three great treatises: an appeal To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation, On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church, and The Freedom of a Christian. That December, when a papal bull threatening excommunication reached him, he burned it publicly outside Wittenberg. The excommunication followed in January 1521.

Worms. In April 1521 he was summoned before the young Emperor Charles V and the princes of the Empire at the Diet of Worms. Shown a table of his books and ordered to recant, he asked for time, and the next day replied that unless he were convinced by Scripture and plain reason, he could not and would not recant, for his conscience was captive to the Word of God. He is remembered as ending, Here I stand, I can do no other; the words may belong to the printed tradition rather than to what was said in the hall, but they fit the man. He was declared an outlaw.

The Wartburg. On the road home he was seized by horsemen — a friendly kidnap arranged by his prince, Frederick the Wise — and hidden in the Wartburg castle above Eisenach. For ten months he lived there as Junker Jörg, Knight George, bearded and restless, often ill and often in deep inner conflict. In a matter of weeks he translated the New Testament from Greek into German. It was published in September 1522, and its vigorous, plain speech helped to shape the German language. The whole Bible followed in 1534.

Troubled years. Returning to Wittenberg in 1522 to calm disorders that had broken out in his absence, he became the leader, often reluctantly, of a movement. He preached, lectured, wrote and organised: German worship, hymns, schools, care for the poor. In 1525 came the Peasants’ War. Luther had rebuked the princes for their oppression and urged peace; when the revolt turned violent he wrote a tract calling on the rulers to strike the rebels down, and many thousands were killed. The same year he wrote The Bondage of the Will against Erasmus.

Katie. On 13 June 1525 he married Katharina von Bora, one of a group of nuns who had escaped from their convent at Easter 1523 and whom Luther had helped to find homes. It was a marriage of conviction more than romance, but it grew into deep affection. They lived in the old Augustinian house in Wittenberg, which Katharina turned into a farm, a brewery, a boarding-house for students and a home for six children, as well as orphaned relatives. Their daughter Elizabeth died as a baby, and their beloved Magdalena at thirteen, in 1542, in her father’s arms. At that table students jotted down his conversation, which became the Table Talk.

Later years. In 1529 he wrote his Small and Large Catechisms, and met Ulrich Zwingli at Marburg, where they agreed on much but parted over the Lord’s Supper. In 1530, still an outlaw, he waited in the fortress of Coburg while his colleague Philip Melanchthon led the evangelical side at the Diet of Augsburg, where the confession Melanchthon had drafted was presented to the Emperor. He lectured on Galatians and on Genesis, wrote hymns and letters of comfort, and suffered from stones, headaches and depression. His last years were darkened by bitterness, and by the writings against the Jews that remain the deepest stain on his name.

Beggars. In January 1546, ill, he travelled to Eisleben to settle a dispute between the counts of Mansfeld. He succeeded, and there, on 18 February, he died. Asked by his friend Justus Jonas whether he stood firm on Christ and the doctrine he had preached, he answered, Yes. On a slip of paper found afterwards he had written, in German and Latin, that we are beggars, and that this is true.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Luther’s road to peace ran through years of fear. If you are in such a season now, tell God so plainly, and ask Him to show you His righteousness as a gift.

2. Staupitz pointed an anxious young man to the wounds of Christ. Is there someone you could point there this week?

3. Luther stood at Worms because his conscience was captive to the Word. Name one place where your conscience is captive to something else — fear of others, comfort, habit.

4. Remember that the same life contains the Wartburg Bible and the tract against the Jews. Pray for grace to finish well.

5. Write down, as Luther did at the last, the truest sentence you know about yourself before God.

A PRAYER
Father, You found Your servant Martin in the storm and in the cloister, and You opened to him the gate of Your righteousness.
Find me where I am afraid, and show me that the righteousness You require is the righteousness You give.
Make my conscience captive to Your Word, and keep me from the bitterness that darkened even his last years.
And when my days are ended, let me die as a beggar who has been made rich in Christ. Amen.

fields.body_html:
Behold, his soul which is lifted up is not upright in him: but the just shall live by his faith. HABAKKUK 2:4

Everything in Luther begins with a single phrase in a single verse, and with a man who was afraid of it. The phrase is the righteousness of God. The verse is Romans 1:17. For years the young professor at Wittenberg could not read it without anger, and when at last he understood it, it opened the whole Bible to him. If you want to understand Luther, you must stand where he stood, in front of that verse, and feel why it frightened him before you can feel why it set him free.

A word he hated

Luther had been taught, as most of his generation were, to hear the righteousness of God as God’s justice: the perfect standard by which He measures every human life and punishes every failure. That is not a false idea. God is just, and Scripture says so on almost every page. But for a conscience like Luther’s, it was a sentence of death. He was trying with all his strength to love God perfectly and to be sorry for his sins perfectly, and he knew that he was doing neither. How could he stand before a righteousness like that?

And enter not into judgment with thy servant: for in thy sight shall no man living be justified. PSALM 143:2

What made it worse was that Paul seemed to say the gospel itself revealed this righteousness. It was bad enough, Luther thought, that the law should crush sinners with God’s justice. Must the gospel do it too? Many years later, in the preface he wrote in 1545 to the collected edition of his Latin writings, he confessed that he had come to hate the phrase, and to be angry with God. It is a startling admission from an old man looking back, and a comforting one. The greatest teacher of grace in his century did not begin as a serene believer. He began as a terrified one.

The whole verse

The key, Luther said, was to read the whole verse and not just the frightening phrase. In the gospel is the righteousness of God revealed from faith to faith; and Paul immediately explains what he means: as it is written, The just shall live by faith. If the righteous person lives by faith, then the righteousness of God in this verse cannot be only a standard to be reached. It must be something given and received — a righteousness by which a merciful God makes the sinner righteous through faith.

But now the righteousness of God without the law is manifested, being witnessed by the law and the prophets; even the righteousness of God which is by faith of Jesus Christ unto all and upon all them that believe. ROMANS 3:21–22

When he saw this, Luther said, he felt as though he had been born again. The whole of Scripture looked different. He went through the Bible in his memory and found the same pattern everywhere: the work of God is what God works in us; the power of God is the power by which He makes us strong; the wisdom of God is the wisdom by which He makes us wise. And the righteousness of God is the righteousness by which He makes us righteous. What had been the most hateful word to him became the sweetest.

A righteousness from outside

In a sermon of 1519 on two kinds of righteousness, Luther called this an alien righteousness — not in the sense of strange, but in the sense of belonging to someone else. It is Christ’s own righteousness, given to us, reckoned to us, laid upon us like a garment. We do not produce it; we receive it. It is not a quality we grow into so that God can then approve of us. It is Christ’s obedience, counted as ours from the moment we believe.

For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him. 2 CORINTHIANS 5:21

This is why he could be so bold in his preaching about sin. In his Easter sermon on Christ’s resurrection, he says that Paul’s words about Christ being raised for our justification do something very simple:

“Here Paul turns my eyes away from my sins and directs them to Christ, for if I look at my sins, they will destroy me.”

That is exactly the turn Luther himself had made. For years he had looked inward, examining his heart for enough love and enough sorrow, and found only more sin. The righteousness of God in the gospel told him to look outward, to Christ, and to find there a righteousness that was complete, perfect and his.

And be found in him, not having mine own righteousness, which is of the law, but that which is through the faith of Christ, the righteousness which is of God by faith. PHILIPPIANS 3:9

Not a new idea

Luther did not think he had invented anything. He found the same teaching in Augustine’s book On the Spirit and the Letter, and he found it throughout the Psalms, which he had lectured on first. He loved the prayers of David that appeal to God’s righteousness not as a threat but as a refuge.

In thee, O LORD, do I put my trust; let me never be ashamed: deliver me in thy righteousness. PSALM 31:1

How could David ask to be delivered by God’s righteousness, if God’s righteousness were only the standard that condemned him? Only if God’s righteousness is also His faithfulness to His promises, His saving justice, the righteousness that puts things right. That is what the prophets meant when they gave the coming King His name.

In his days Judah shall be saved, and Israel shall dwell safely: and this is his name whereby he shall be called, THE LORD OUR RIGHTEOUSNESS. JEREMIAH 23:6

Reading the story with care

Two cautions belong here. First, Luther told the story of his discovery decades after the event, and he told it as a single moment of breakthrough. Historians have argued for a century about when it happened, and it is likely that his understanding grew over several years of lecturing rather than arriving in one afternoon. That does not make the discovery less real. Most of God’s great mercies to us are slow before they are sudden.

Second, Luther sometimes painted the teachers who went before him more darkly than they deserved. Not every medieval preacher taught that sinners must earn their righteousness; Staupitz, his own superior, pointed him to Christ, and Bernard of Clairvaux, whom Luther loved, had preached grace warmly. The problem Luther faced was real, and the practice of the church around him was often worse than its best theology. But it is fair to say that he recovered something that had been obscured, not something that had been wholly lost.

For they being ignorant of God’s righteousness, and going about to establish their own righteousness, have not submitted themselves unto the righteousness of God. ROMANS 10:3

That last verse names the danger in every age, including our own. We are always going about to establish our own righteousness — by religious effort, by moral achievement, by comparing ourselves favourably with others. The gospel asks us to stop, and submit to a righteousness we did not make. It is the hardest thing in the world for a proud heart, and the sweetest thing in the world for a broken one.

1. Read Romans 1:16–17 slowly three times. Underline the word faith each time it appears, and ask what the verse says God gives.

3. When you next feel condemned by your sins, practise Luther’s turn: say aloud, “My sins are real, but my righteousness is in Christ,” and look to Him.

4. Pray Psalm 31:1 each morning this week, asking God to deliver you in His righteousness.

5. If you have been slow to understand grace, take heart from Luther’s long years of struggle, and keep reading Scripture until it opens.

Thank You that in the gospel Your righteousness is revealed as a gift, and that Christ, who knew no sin, was made sin for me.
Turn my eyes from my sins to my Saviour, and let me find in Him a righteousness that is complete.
Deliver me in Your righteousness, and teach me to live by faith, through Jesus Christ, the Lord our Righteousness. Amen.

fields.title: Faith Alone
fields.body_html:
Therefore we conclude that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law. ROMANS 3:28

When Luther translated Romans into German at the Wartburg, he came to Paul’s great conclusion in the third chapter — that a man is justified by faith without the deeds of the law — and added a word. In his German the verse says that a man is justified by faith alone. His enemies pounced: he had tampered with Scripture. Luther replied, in a lively little book of 1530 on translating, that the word alone was not in the Greek, but the sense was, and that a German who wished to say what Paul said would have to put it in. Whatever one thinks of the translation, the word stuck. Faith alone became the banner of the Reformation.

What faith is

It matters enormously what Luther meant by faith, because the phrase is easily misheard. He did not mean believing that certain facts are true. He was blunt about that. Preaching on the birth of Christ, he says that merely believing the history is worth nothing, for even the damned believe it. True faith, he says, is this:

“The right and gracious faith which God demands is, that you firmly believe that Christ is born for you, and that this birth took place for your welfare.”

Faith, for Luther, is trust. It is the heart’s leaning its whole weight on Christ and His promise. It is the empty hand that receives what God gives. That is why faith does not compete with grace as a kind of work of our own. Faith contributes nothing except its emptiness. It is simply the way a beggar takes bread.

But to him that worketh not, but believeth on him that justifieth the ungodly, his faith is counted for righteousness. ROMANS 4:5

Notice the startling phrase in that verse: him that justifieth the ungodly. God does not justify people once they have become godly. He justifies the ungodly, and godliness follows. Luther never tired of this. In The Freedom of a Christian he compares faith to a wedding ring: in the marriage of the soul to Christ, all that is the soul’s — its sin, its death, its damnation — becomes Christ’s, and all that is Christ’s — His righteousness, life and salvation — becomes the soul’s. He called it a happy exchange.

For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. EPHESIANS 2:8–9

Why alone?

Why did Luther insist on the word alone? Because anything added to faith as a condition of our acceptance destroys it. If I am justified by faith plus my sorrow, I must ask whether my sorrow is deep enough. If by faith plus my love, whether my love is pure enough. If by faith plus my good works, whether I have done enough. Every addition sends the conscience back into the anxious self-examination from which the gospel came to rescue it. Luther had lived there for years. He knew there was no floor to it.

Knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law, but by the faith of Jesus Christ, even we have believed in Jesus Christ, that we might be justified by the faith of Christ, and not by the works of the law: for by the works of the law shall no flesh be justified. GALATIANS 2:16

So faith alone is not a narrow slogan. It is a pastoral mercy. It says to the trembling conscience: your standing with God does not rest on anything in you, not even on the strength of your faith, but on Christ, whom faith receives. Weak faith holding a strong Christ is saved as surely as strong faith.

Therefore being justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ. ROMANS 5:1

Faith that works

But Luther was just as clear that faith alone is never alone. The faith that justifies is a living thing, and it cannot help but love. In his preface to Romans, written in 1522, he describes faith as a lively, busy, active power that does good works before anyone has asked whether it ought to — the very words that, read aloud in a London meeting-room in 1738, warmed the heart of John Wesley. In his sermon on the appearing of the grace of God, he puts it in a single line:

“He is not idle; for faith is never inactive.”

The order matters. Good works do not make a person good; a good person does good works. A tree does not become good by bearing fruit; it bears fruit because it is good. In his sermon on Paul’s praise of love, Luther turns this into a firm rule against those who said faith needs love to complete it:

“Justification of necessity precedes love. One does not love until he has become godly and righteous. Love does not make us godly, but when one has become godly love is the result.”

For in Jesus Christ neither circumcision availeth any thing, nor uncircumcision; but faith which worketh by love. GALATIANS 5:6

An honest qualification

Luther’s zeal for faith alone sometimes carried him too far in his judgement of other parts of Scripture. In the preface to his New Testament of 1522 he called the Epistle of James an epistle of straw compared with the letters that preach Christ most clearly, because he thought it set works against faith. He was wrong about James, and later editions of his preface quietly dropped the phrase. James is not opposed to Paul. He is opposing a dead faith that says the words and does nothing, which is exactly what Luther opposed too.

Even so faith, if it hath not works, is dead, being alone. JAMES 2:17

Paul and James use the word justify in different ways, and they are fighting different enemies. Paul is fighting those who would add works to faith as the ground of acceptance; James is fighting those who would use faith as an excuse for doing nothing. Luther’s own sermons, full of the love of neighbour, show that at his best he knew this. We need both apostles. The faith that justifies is the faith that works.

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me. GALATIANS 2:20

That last verse was one of Luther’s favourites, and he loved its final words most of all: who loved me, and gave himself for me. It is faith alone that can say them. And it is faith alone that, having said them, goes out gladly to love.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Finish the sentence honestly: “God accepts me because …” If anything other than Christ creeps in, cross it out and write His name.

2. Notice whether you treat your faith as a work — worrying whether it is strong enough. Turn your attention from your faith to its object.

3. Read Luther’s picture of the happy exchange and list what Christ has taken from you and what He has given you.

4. Choose one practical act of love for a neighbour this week, done not to earn anything but because you have already received everything.

5. Read the second chapter of James alongside Romans 4, and thank God that both apostles are in your Bible.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus, I come to You with empty hands, for I have nothing to bring but my need.
Thank You that You justify the ungodly, and that my standing before the Father rests on You and not on me.
Where my faith is weak, hold me fast; where I am tempted to add my works to Your grace, humble me.
And let the faith You give me be busy in love, so that my neighbour may taste the kindness You have shown to me. Amen.

fields.title: The Theology of the Cross
fields.body_html:
But God forbid that I should glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by whom the world is crucified unto me, and I unto the world. GALATIANS 6:14

In April 1518, six months after the theses on indulgences, Luther travelled on foot to Heidelberg to take part in a disputation held by his own Augustinian order. His superiors hoped he would be quiet about indulgences, and he was. Instead he put forward a set of theses on something deeper: how human beings come to know God at all. Among them are a handful of sentences that have shaped Christian thought ever since. There are, Luther said, two kinds of theologians. There is the theologian of glory, and there is the theologian of the cross.

Two ways of looking for God

The theologian of glory, as Luther describes him in the Heidelberg Disputation, looks for God in power, success, wisdom and visible achievement. He reasons upward from what he can see in the world and in himself to what God must be like. He assumes that God is found at the top — in the strong, the clever, the moral, the admired. And he assumes that his own good works will carry him up towards God. He is, in the end, a man who calls good evil and evil good, because he despises the cross and loves his own works.

fields.body_html:
For the law was given by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Christ. JOHN 1:17

Luther once said, in effect, that whoever knows how to tell the law from the gospel rightly may thank God and know that he is a theologian. It sounds like a modest skill. It is in fact, he believed, the hardest thing in the Christian life, and the most important. Almost every error in the church, and almost every trouble of the anxious conscience, comes from confusing the two: turning the gospel into a new law, or turning the law into a way of salvation. Get the distinction right, and the whole Bible opens. Get it wrong, and you will either despair or grow proud.

Two words from one God

Both law and gospel are God’s Word, and both run through the whole Bible, Old Testament and New. The law is everything in Scripture that tells us what we must do and be: love God with all your heart, love your neighbour as yourself, do not covet. The gospel is everything that tells us what God has done and gives in Christ: your sins are forgiven, Christ died for you, He was raised for your justification. The law commands; the gospel promises. The law says, do this; the gospel says, it is done.

Wherefore the law is holy, and the commandment holy, and just, and good. ROMANS 7:12

Luther never despised the law. It is holy, just and good, because it comes from God and describes a life of love. The problem is not with the law but with us. We cannot keep it, and the law cannot give us the power to keep it. It can show us the way, but it cannot carry us down it.

What the law does

Luther taught that the law has more than one use. In the world it acts like a bridle, restraining wickedness through fear of punishment, so that society can function; this is its civil use. But its chief spiritual work is to be a mirror. It shows us our sin. It strips away our illusions about ourselves, and drives us to despair of our own righteousness. He calls this its proper, theological work.

Therefore by the deeds of the law there shall no flesh be justified in his sight: for by the law is the knowledge of sin. ROMANS 3:20

In his Easter sermon, meditating on Paul’s words that the strength of sin is the law, Luther puts it briefly: “The more clearly we understand the law, the more sin oppresses and stings us.” That is not a failure of the law. It is the law doing its job. A man who does not know he is ill will never go to the physician. The law makes us know it.

Wherefore the law was our schoolmaster to bring us unto Christ, that we might be justified by faith. GALATIANS 3:24

The letter and the Spirit

Luther’s Pentecost sermon on the office of the Holy Spirit develops this with great beauty. Pentecost, he points out, was the Jewish feast that remembered the giving of the law at Sinai, fifty days after the Passover. On the Christian Pentecost, fifty days after Easter, God gave a different kind of law: not written on stone, but written by the Spirit on the heart. The written law, Luther says, stays outside us. It commands, but the heart resents it, and at best it produces fearful, outward obedience. He concludes:

“Hence we see that the Law, as long as it is merely written, a Law in letters, makes no one righteous, for it enters not the heart.”

The Spirit does what the letter cannot. Through the preaching of Christ, He writes on the heart, sets it on fire, and makes a new person who loves God and gladly does His will. Luther insists that this is the real difference between the two: not that the gospel asks less, but that the gospel gives what the law demands.

Who also hath made us able ministers of the new testament; not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life. 2 CORINTHIANS 3:6
I will put my law in their inward parts, and write it in their hearts; and will be their God, and they shall be my people. JEREMIAH 31:33

This is why, in the same sermon, Luther says that preaching the law alone accomplishes nothing: “For, briefly, there must first be love in the heart, otherwise nothing is accomplished in keeping the Law.” And love comes only from the Spirit, through the gospel.

Keeping them distinct

So the preacher, and every Christian, must learn to use the right word at the right time. To the proud and careless, speak the law, that they may see their need. To the broken and terrified, speak the gospel, and speak nothing else. It is cruel to lay the law on a conscience already crushed, and foolish to offer cheap comfort to someone who is not yet sorry. Luther saw both mistakes all around him. Medieval preaching, he believed, had too often turned Christ into a new Moses, a stern judge whose commands must be satisfied. Some of his own followers, on the other hand, began to preach grace to people who had never felt their sin.

For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth. ROMANS 10:4

An honest caution

Luther’s language here is sometimes so bold that it can mislead. In the Pentecost sermon he says that the Holy Spirit comes to abolish the letter of the law, and that Christians are not to be governed by laws. Read alone, such phrases could suggest that the commandments no longer matter for believers. That is not what Luther meant, and he had to fight it in his own lifetime. In the late 1530s his former student Johann Agricola began to teach that the law should not be preached in the church at all, and Luther opposed him firmly. The Christian, he insisted, is still a sinner as well as righteous, and the old Adam still needs the law’s mirror and the law’s bridle. His own catechism begins with the Ten Commandments.

What shall we say then? Shall we continue in sin, that grace may abound? God forbid. ROMANS 6:1–2

Lutheran and Reformed teachers after him debated whether the law also has a third use, as a guide for the believer’s grateful obedience. Whatever one’s view, both sides agree on the heart of the matter. The law cannot justify, and it is not the gospel. But the gospel does not abolish the good will of God. It writes it on the heart.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Read the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20 as a mirror. Which one shows you most clearly your need of Christ?

2. Then read Romans 8:1–4 and hear the gospel spoken directly to that need.

3. Notice whether you tend to hear the gospel as a new set of demands. Ask God to let you hear it as good news.

4. If you teach or lead others, consider whether you speak more law or more gospel, and whether you speak the right word to the right person.

5. Pray for the Spirit to write God’s law on your heart, so that you do gladly what you once did only from fear.

A PRAYER
Holy Father, Your law is holy and just and good, and it shows me how far I have fallen short.
Thank You that You have not left me with the letter that kills, but have given me Your Spirit who gives life.
Teach me to hear Your law as a mirror that drives me to Christ, and Your gospel as the promise that rests in Him.
Write Your will upon my heart, and let me love what You command, for the sake of Jesus Christ, the end of the law for all who believe. Amen.

fields.title: Lord of All, Servant of All
fields.body_html:
For though I be free from all men, yet have I made myself servant unto all, that I might gain the more. 1 CORINTHIANS 9:19

In the autumn of 1520, with a papal bull threatening excommunication already on its way to him, Luther wrote the gentlest of his great treatises. The Freedom of a Christian was sent to Pope Leo X with a letter, and it is short, calm and pastoral. It contains no abuse and little controversy. It is simply an explanation of what it means to be a Christian, and it rests on two statements that seem, at first, to contradict each other. A Christian, Luther says in effect, is a free lord over all things, subject to no one; and a Christian is a willing servant of all, subject to everyone. The whole Christian life, he believed, lies in holding both together.

Free in faith

The first statement concerns the inner person, the soul before God. Nothing outward can make the soul righteous or free: not fasting, not holy places, not priestly robes, not religious duties. Only one thing is needed for the Christian life, and that is the Word of God, the gospel of Christ. When the soul believes that Word, it receives everything the Word promises. It is united to Christ as a bride to her husband, and it shares in all He has.

If the Son therefore shall make you free, ye shall be free indeed. JOHN 8:36

That is why the believer is lord of all. Not that he owns the world or commands it, but that nothing in it can harm his standing with God. Sin, death, the law and the devil have no claim on the one who belongs to Christ. Luther says the same in his Pentecost sermon, where he describes how the Spirit teaches the heart to cry out that Christ is Lord over all things, and asks, in the believer’s voice: “My Lord Christ, who takes my part, is lord over all things; what shall harm me?”

For all things are yours; whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come; all are yours; and ye are Christ’s; and Christ is God’s. 1 CORINTHIANS 3:21–23

This freedom has a practical side that Luther loved to press. The Christian is free from man-made rules about food, clothing, days and seasons as ways of pleasing God. In his sermon on the appearing of the grace of God he attacks those who make holiness a matter of special garments, special diets and special times, and says of all such things: “In all these things, everyone is given freedom, if only they be used in soberness, or moderation.” Eat, drink and dress with thanks, he says, and guard only against excess.

Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free, and be not entangled again with the yoke of bondage. GALATIANS 5:1

Servant in love

But a Christian does not live only in his soul. He lives in a body, among other people, and here the second statement comes into play. Because he is already rich in Christ, he has no need to do good works to earn anything. He is therefore free to do them entirely for his neighbour’s sake. Luther’s memorable phrase in The Freedom of a Christian is that each believer should become, as it were, a Christ to his neighbour — giving himself to others as Christ gave Himself to him.

His Christmas sermon puts it in almost the same way. Having received Christ as your own, he says, “it follows that you will do good works by doing to your neighbour as Christ has done to you.” And he sums up the two sides of the Christian life in a few words: “He loves, we believe, thus both are united into one.” Christ loves us, and we receive Him by faith; our neighbour needs us, and we serve him in love.

Let this mind be in you, which was also in Christ Jesus: who, being in the form of God, thought it not robbery to be equal with God: but made himself of no reputation, and took upon him the form of a servant. PHILIPPIANS 2:5–7

This love is not vague. Luther is scathing about religious works that help no one: gold in the churches, bells, candles, masses said for the dead, while the poor man lies at the door. In the sermon on the appearing of grace he says simply: “Look to your neighbor. There you will find enough to do, a thousand kind offices to render.” The freedom of faith is not freedom from others. It is freedom for them.

Owe no man any thing, but to love one another: for he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law. ROMANS 13:8

Why both are needed

If we keep only the first statement, freedom becomes selfishness. If we keep only the second, service becomes slavery, a new law by which we try to earn God’s favour. fields.body_html:
Jesus answered them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin. JOHN 8:34

In 1524 the most famous scholar in Europe entered the argument. Desiderius Erasmus of Rotterdam, the editor of the Greek New Testament that Luther had used for his translation, had long sympathised with calls for reform, but he disliked Luther’s violence and feared his certainty. Pressed to take a side, he published a Diatribe on Free Will, a courteous, learned and moderate book arguing that human beings retain some small power to turn towards God or away from Him. Luther replied late in 1525 with The Bondage of the Will. It is the longest and fiercest of his theological works, and one of the most important. Late in life, he is remembered as saying that of all his books he would gladly see only this one and his catechism survive.

The heart of the matter

Luther began by thanking Erasmus. Everyone else, he said in effect, had attacked him on side issues — the papacy, purgatory, indulgences. Erasmus alone had gone to the hinge on which everything turns: the question of what the human will can do before God. Luther was right that this is the hinge. If fallen human beings can contribute something, however small, to their own salvation, then salvation is a partnership, and grace is God’s help to our effort. If they cannot, then salvation is wholly God’s work, and grace is everything.

There is none righteous, no, not one: there is none that understandeth, there is none that seeketh after God. ROMANS 3:10–11

Luther did not deny that people make choices. We choose what to eat, whom to marry, how to work. In the things below us, he granted, we have a real freedom. But in the things of God — in turning to Him, trusting Him, loving Him — the fallen will is not free. It is bound. Not bound by force, as though we wanted God but were prevented, but bound by its own desires. We do what we want, and what we want, left to ourselves, is not God.

A captive will

Luther’s sermons say the same thing more briefly and warmly. In his sermon on the appearing of the grace of God, commenting on Paul’s words that Christ gave Himself to redeem us, he reasons simply: if Christ came to redeem us, we must have been captives.

“If we claim there is aught in us not bound in sin, we disparage the grace whereby, according to the Gospel, we are redeemed.”

And in the same sermon, looking at human reluctance to face the day of judgement, he asks pointedly: “Where, then, does human nature stand? where reason? where the free-will so much extolled as inclined to and potent for good?”

And you hath he quickened, who were dead in trespasses and sins. EPHESIANS 2:1

In The Bondage of the Will Luther uses a vivid, and much-debated, picture. The human will, he says, is like a beast of burden standing between two riders. If God rides it, it goes where God wills; if Satan rides it, it goes where Satan wills. It cannot choose its rider; the riders contend for it. The picture is meant to show that the will is never neutral, never poised in the middle choosing freely between God and sin. It is always already carried somewhere.

No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day. JOHN 6:44

Why it comforts

To many readers this sounds grim. Luther thought it the most comforting of doctrines. If my salvation depended on my will, he said, I could never be sure of it; amid so many temptations and dangers I would certainly lose it, and even if I did not, I would never know whether I had done enough. But because it depends on God’s will and God’s promise, I can be certain. My perseverance rests not on my strength but on His faithfulness.

For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. PHILIPPIANS 2:13

The bondage of the will also humbles us in the right way. It takes away every ground of boasting. And it teaches us to pray. If I cannot turn my own heart, then I must ask God to turn it. Luther’s whole life of prayer grew from this conviction.

A new heart also will I give you, and a new spirit will I put within you: and I will take away the stony heart out of your flesh, and I will give you an heart of flesh. EZEKIEL 36:26

The hidden and the revealed God

The hardest part of the book comes when Luther faces the question that always follows. If God alone can turn the will, why does He not turn every will? Luther’s answer is to distinguish between God hidden and God revealed. There is, he says, a hidden will of God that we cannot search out, and we must not try. Our business is with God as He has revealed Himself in His Word — above all in Christ, who weeps over Jerusalem and invites all who labour to come to Him. Flee the hidden God, Luther counsels, and run to the God who is preached, clothed in His promises.

The secret things belong unto the LORD our God: but those things which are revealed belong unto us and to our children for ever. DEUTERONOMY 29:29

Reading it with care

The Bondage of the Will must be read with care. Luther wrote it in the heat of controversy, and he sometimes pressed his language of necessity so hard that he seemed to make God the author of everything that happens in a way Scripture itself does not. His own closest colleague, Philip Melanchthon, later softened his teaching on the will, and the Lutheran churches in their later confession steered carefully between Luther’s sharpest statements and Erasmus’s position. Many devout readers of Scripture, in every tradition, have believed that Luther went too far.

It must also be said that Erasmus had real points. He feared that such teaching would make people careless or despairing, and he loved the moral seriousness of the Gospels. Luther treated him with contempt he did not deserve. But on the main point — that salvation is from first to last the gift of God, and that we contribute nothing to it but the sin from which we need to be saved — Luther stood with Paul and with Augustine.

So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy. ROMANS 9:16
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where do you still quietly believe that your salvation rests partly on your own willingness? Confess it, and thank God that He drew you.

2. If there is someone you long to see turn to Christ, stop trying to argue their will into faith and begin to pray daily that God would give them a new heart.

3. When your own heart feels cold, pray Philippians 2:13, asking God to work in you both to will and to do.

4. If you have been troubled by questions about God’s hidden will, take Luther’s advice: turn from speculation to the Christ of the gospels, and read one of His invitations aloud.

5. Consider how you argue with people you disagree with. Learn from Luther’s strength, but not from his contempt.

Lord God, I confess that left to myself I would never have sought You, for my will was bound by my own desires.
Thank You that You drew me, quickened me when I was dead, and gave me a new heart.
Keep me from prying into what You have hidden, and hold me fast to what You have revealed in Your Son.
Work in me both to will and to do Your good pleasure, and let all the glory of my salvation be Yours alone. Amen.

fields.title: The Word Alone
fields.body_html:
The grass withereth, the flower fadeth: but the word of our God shall stand for ever. ISAIAH 40:8

When Luther came back from the Wartburg to Wittenberg in March 1522, the town was in turmoil. In his absence, zealous reformers had smashed images, forced changes in worship and frightened the weak. Luther, still an outlaw, preached eight sermons on eight days, and calmed the city. In one of them he said something that goes to the root of his whole method. He had opposed indulgences and the papacy, he said, but never with force. He had simply taught, preached and written God’s Word, and otherwise done nothing. And while he slept, or sat drinking Wittenberg beer with his friends Philip and Amsdorf, the Word had done it all.

The power is in the Word

That was not false modesty. Luther genuinely believed that the Word of God is alive and does its own work. The preacher’s task is not to manipulate, compel or impress, but to speak what God has spoken and let it go to work. In his Easter sermon on the resurrection he describes the Word’s power in the believing heart as strong enough to conquer death, the devil and sin, and then adds one of his most striking lines: “So mighty is the Word that God himself would sooner be vanquished than that his Word should be conquered.”

So shall my word be that goeth forth out of my mouth: it shall not return unto me void, but it shall accomplish that which I please, and it shall prosper in the thing whereto I sent it. ISAIAH 55:11

This is why he gave his life to preaching, lecturing and translating. It is why he wanted every German to have the Bible in German. And it is why he could be so calm, in some moods, about the future of the Reformation. It was not his cause. It was the Word’s.

Is not my word like as a fire? saith the LORD; and like a hammer that breaketh the rock in pieces? JEREMIAH 23:29

Scripture alone

In the debates with Rome, this confidence took the form of a principle: Scripture alone is the final authority for faith. Popes, councils and church fathers were to be honoured, but they could err, and had erred; only Scripture could not. That was what Luther said at Worms. His conscience, he said, was captive to the Word of God, and unless he could be shown from Scripture and plain reason that he was wrong, he could not recant.

His Christmas sermon on the birth of Jesus has a beautiful picture of this. The angel told the shepherds that the sign would be a babe wrapped in swaddling clothes. Luther reads the swaddling clothes as the Scriptures:

“The clothes are nothing else than the holy Scriptures, in which the Christian truth lies wrapped, in which the faith is described.”

And a little later, he draws the conclusion: “for there is no other testimony on earth concerning Christian truth than the holy Scriptures.” We find Christ where God has wrapped Him — in the Bible, and nowhere else so surely.

And this shall be a sign unto you; Ye shall find the babe wrapped in swaddling clothes, lying in a manger. LUKE 2:12

Christ the centre

For Luther, Scripture is not a collection of rules or proof texts. It is a book about Christ. The Old Testament, he said, is the cradle in which Christ lies; the New Testament opens it and shows Him to us. He found Christ in the promises to Abraham, in the sacrifices, in the Psalms, in the prophets. And he gave a famous test for judging the books of the Bible: whether they preach and promote Christ.

And beginning at Moses and all the prophets, he expounded unto them in all the scriptures the things concerning himself. LUKE 24:27
Search the scriptures; for in them ye think ye have eternal life: and they are they which testify of me. JOHN 5:39

This Christ-centred reading kept Luther from dry literalism and from endless allegory. When he read the Bible, he was always asking where the gospel was, where the promise was, where Christ was.

The Word heard

Luther also insisted that the Word is first of all a spoken word, a word proclaimed and heard. Faith, Paul says, comes by hearing. The church, Luther said, is not a pen-house but a mouth-house: God’s Word is meant to be preached aloud, into ears, so that it can reach hearts. His sermon on the appearing of grace says that Christ is not placed in your hand or your bosom, but offered to your heart through your ears, in the Word.

So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God. ROMANS 10:17

The same sermon adds that the Word has two uses, taken from the builders of Jerusalem in Nehemiah who worked with one hand and held a sword in the other. We are, Luther says, “to make a twofold use of the Word of God: as both bread and weapon; for feeding and for resisting; in peace and in war.” It feeds the soul, and it defends the soul against the devil and error.

For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword. HEBREWS 4:12

Honest cautions

Three cautions are needed. First, Scripture alone did not mean, for Luther, Scripture read alone. He read the Bible with Augustine and Bernard at his elbow, he kept the ancient creeds, and he fought hard against those who claimed private revelations of the Spirit apart from the written Word. The principle has sometimes been turned into an excuse for every individual to make his own Bible. Luther would have been horrified.

Second, Luther’s test of whether a book promotes Christ led him to rank some books of the New Testament below others. He placed Hebrews, James, Jude and Revelation together at the end of his New Testament and wrote cautious prefaces to them. The church has not followed him in this, and rightly. The canon is God’s gift to us, not ours to rearrange by our own taste.

Third, his readings of the Old Testament were sometimes more ingenious than sound, as in the same Christmas sermon where the coarse outer swaddling cloth becomes the law and the linen inner cloth the prophets. The point he makes is true; the method is not one to copy.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Do you believe that God’s Word has power in itself? Choose one passage this week and simply read it aloud to someone, trusting it to do its work.

2. When you read the Bible, ask Luther’s question each time: where is Christ here, and where is the promise?

3. Take hearing seriously. Sit under the preaching of the Word this Sunday as if God were speaking to you, because He is.

4. Use the Word as a weapon: learn one verse by heart to answer a temptation you often face.

5. Read the Bible with the wider church — the creeds, a trustworthy commentary, older Christians — rather than alone.

A PRAYER
Lord God, Your word stands for ever, and it does not return to You empty.
Thank You for wrapping Christ in the Scriptures, and for giving them to us in our own tongue.
Make me a humble hearer of Your Word, and let it be bread to feed me and a sword to defend me.
Keep my conscience captive to what You have said, and show me Christ on every page. Amen.

fields.title: A Priesthood of All Believers
fields.body_html:
But ye are a chosen generation, a royal priesthood, an holy nation, a peculiar people; that ye should shew forth the praises of him who hath called you out of darkness into his marvellous light. 1 PETER 2:9

In the summer of 1520 Luther published an appeal To the Christian Nobility of the German Nation. It was written in German, for laymen, and it sold in thousands within days. In it he argued that the Roman church had built three walls around itself to prevent any reform. The first wall was the claim that the clergy are a spiritual estate, set above the laity, so that no layman may ever correct a priest or a pope. Luther knocked that wall down with a single teaching that has shaped Protestant life ever since: every baptised Christian is a priest.

One estate

The medieval church divided Christians into two estates. There was the spiritual estate — pope, bishops, priests, monks and nuns — and the temporal estate — princes, merchants, craftsmen and farmers. The first was thought to be nearer to God, holier in itself, and the proper keeper of the sacraments and the Scriptures. Luther said that this division had no ground in the Bible. All Christians, he argued, belong to the spiritual estate, because all have one baptism, one gospel, one faith, and are all alike Christians. It is baptism, not ordination, that makes a person a priest.

Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood, and hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father; to him be glory and dominion for ever and ever. Amen. REVELATION 1:5–6

This did not mean that there should be no pastors. Luther was clear that, because all have the same right, no one should take the public office of preaching and administering the sacraments without being called to it by the community. The minister is not a higher kind of Christian, but a Christian set apart to serve others in a particular office, as a mayor is a citizen chosen to govern his fellow citizens. If he is removed from office, he is what he was before: a baptised believer like everyone else.

Access to God

At the heart of this teaching is a simple and glorious truth. No Christian needs a human go-between to reach God. There is one mediator, the Lord Jesus Christ, and every believer may come to the Father directly through Him.

For there is one God, and one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus. 1 TIMOTHY 2:5
Let us therefore come boldly unto the throne of grace, that we may obtain mercy, and find grace to help in time of need. HEBREWS 4:16

For ordinary people in Luther’s day, this was a liberation. They could read the Bible for themselves, in German. They could pray to God in their own words, without the saints as intermediaries. They could receive the assurance of forgiveness from the promise of the gospel. They could even hear another Christian’s confession and speak Christ’s forgiveness to them. Luther valued private confession highly, but he insisted that any believer could speak the word of absolution to a troubled brother or sister.

Confess your faults one to another, and pray one for another, that ye may be healed. JAMES 5:16

Priests for one another

It is easy to misunderstand the priesthood of all believers as a kind of spiritual individualism: every man his own priest, needing no one. That is the opposite of what Luther meant. A priest is someone who stands before God on behalf of others. To say that every Christian is a priest is to say that every Christian is responsible for his neighbour — to pray for him, to teach him, to comfort him, to bring him God’s Word.

Luther’s Christmas sermon makes this point from the shepherds at Bethlehem. Why, he asks, were the first hearers of the gospel shepherds? His answer:

“That there were shepherds, means that no one is to hear the Gospel for himself alone, but every one is to tell it to others who are not acquainted with it.”

He goes on to say that each believer should seek to bring others to faith, so that one may be a shepherd of the other, leading him into the pasture of the gospel. Every Christian, in other words, has a ministry.

Bear ye one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ. GALATIANS 6:2

Every Christian also has a sacrifice to offer. Not the sacrifice of the Mass, which Luther rejected as a work offered to God, but the sacrifice of praise, and of the whole life given in service.

I beseech you therefore, brethren, by the mercies of God, that ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God, which is your reasonable service. ROMANS 12:1

Where the teaching went

The priesthood of all believers set loose enormous energies. It led to the German Bible, to congregational singing, to household catechising, to the dignity of lay vocation that the next chapter describes. It gave generations of ordinary Christians the confidence to read, pray and speak about God without asking permission.

But it must also be said that Luther’s practice did not always match his principle. When the Reformation met disorder — radical preachers, iconoclasts, the Anabaptists and the Peasants’ War — he grew cautious. He insisted more and more on the ordered, called ministry, and he looked to the Christian princes to organise and oversee the new churches, which he called a temporary emergency measure. The emergency lasted for centuries. In many Lutheran lands the prince became, in effect, the head of the church, and the priesthood of believers was not always visible in parishes run by the state. Luther cannot be blamed for everything that followed, but he did not guard his own teaching as well as he might have done.

How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? ROMANS 10:14

The balance he struck in principle is still the right one. The whole church is a priesthood, and the church also needs preachers, called and sent, to proclaim the Word publicly. The two do not compete. The preacher serves the priesthood; the priesthood hears the preacher and carries the Word into every home and workplace.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Thank God that you may come to Him directly through Christ. Pray today without any sense that you need permission.

2. Name one person for whom you are a priest — someone you can pray for, teach or comfort. Do one of these things this week.

3. If someone confides a sin to you, practise speaking Christ’s forgiveness to them plainly from Scripture.

4. Honour your pastor as a fellow believer called to an office, and pray for him or her by name.

5. Ask whether you have treated your faith as a private possession. Tell the gospel to someone who does not know it.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, our one Mediator and great High Priest, You have washed us in Your blood and made us priests to Your Father.
Thank You that I may come boldly to the throne of grace, and that no one stands between me and You.
Make me a priest for others — quick to pray, ready to comfort, glad to speak Your Word.
Bless those You have called to preach, and let Your whole church show forth the praises of Him who called us into His marvellous light. Amen.

fields.title: Holy Work in Ordinary Places
fields.body_html:
And whatsoever ye do, do it heartily, as to the Lord, and not unto men. COLOSSIANS 3:23

When Luther was a boy, a calling meant one thing. To have a vocation was to be called out of ordinary life into the monastery or the priesthood. Monks and nuns were said to follow the counsels of perfection; everyone else lived a lower, secular life, which might be decent but was not truly holy. Luther had believed this so deeply that he broke his father’s heart to enter the cloister. Some of his most lasting work was to turn it upside down. By the end of his life the German word for calling, Beruf, had come to mean what it still means: a person’s ordinary work and station in life, seen as a place where God has put them to serve.

No higher road

In 1521, at the Wartburg, Luther wrote a book On Monastic Vows. He argued that vows made in the belief that they would earn salvation, or make a person holier than other Christians, were contrary to faith. There is no higher road to God than the one every Christian walks, the road of faith in Christ and love for the neighbour. The monk in his cell is not nearer to God, simply because he is a monk, than the maid in the kitchen or the farmer in the field.

His sermon on the appearing of the grace of God tells a story from the desert fathers to make the point. A monk who could not bear the temptations of his community fled to the wilderness to serve God in peace. But there, when his water-jug kept tipping over, he flew into a rage and smashed it. He realised that the trouble lay in himself, not in his surroundings, and went back. Luther draws the moral:

“Conflict and not flight, energy and not rest, must be the order in this life if we are to win the crown.”

Holiness is not found by running away from ordinary life. It is lived out in the middle of it.

Let every man abide in the same calling wherein he was called. 1 CORINTHIANS 7:20

God at work behind masks

Luther loved to say that God hides Himself behind the ordinary work of human beings as behind a mask. God could feed us directly, as He fed Israel with manna; instead He feeds us through the farmer, the miller and the baker. He could protect us directly; instead He does it through parents, magistrates and neighbours. When we pray for our daily bread, He answers by setting a whole world of people to work.

The eyes of all wait upon thee; and thou givest them their meat in due season. Thou openest thine hand, and satisfiest the desire of every living thing. PSALM 145:15–16

This means that the most ordinary work is a sharing in God’s own care for His world. The mother feeding her child, the carpenter framing a roof, the clerk keeping honest accounts, the soldier guarding a city, the teacher explaining a sum — all are God’s hands. Their work is holy, not because it is religious, but because God is in it, serving the neighbour through them.

Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it: except the LORD keep the city, the watchman waketh but in vain. PSALM 127:1

For the neighbour’s sake

If God does not need our good works, who does? Our neighbour does. This is the other half of Luther’s teaching on vocation, and it flows straight from justification by faith. Because we are accepted freely in Christ, we do not work to earn God’s favour. We are free to point all our work outward, towards the people who need it. His Christmas sermon puts it plainly: having received Christ, you have no other way to serve Him than “so to direct your works that they may be of benefit to your neighbour, just as the works of Christ are of benefit and use to you.”

In that same sermon he paints Mary and Joseph on the road to Bethlehem, very likely without a servant, Joseph doing the work of both master and servant, Mary of both mistress and maid. There is no hint of shame in it. The Holy Family did ordinary work, and did it on the very road along which God was bringing His Son into the world.

With good will doing service, as to the Lord, and not to men. EPHESIANS 6:7

In a little book on marriage written in 1522, Luther imagines a father washing his baby’s nappies while clever people mock him as a fool. God and the angels, Luther says, smile at the sight — not because nappies are holy in themselves, but because the father is doing it in faith. That is the whole doctrine of vocation in a single picture.

Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God. 1 CORINTHIANS 10:31

The cross in our calling

Vocation is not always pleasant. Luther knew that every calling carries its own cross: the farmer’s weather, the parent’s sleepless nights, the magistrate’s hard decisions, the servant’s unjust master. He believed that we do not need to invent crosses by going on pilgrimages or taking extraordinary vows. God lays enough on us in our daily work. The Christian bears it with patience, trusting that God is using it both to serve others and to shape him.

Whatsoever thy hand findeth to do, do it with thy might. ECCLESIASTES 9:10

Honest cautions

Luther’s teaching on vocation has a shadow side. He tended to see a person’s calling as fixed by birth and circumstance: the peasant should remain a peasant, the servant a servant. Taken that way, it can become a way of keeping people in their place and silencing their longing for justice or change. Paul’s counsel to abide in one’s calling is immediately followed, in the same passage, by his advice to the slave to take his freedom if he can. Scripture does not sanctify every social arrangement.

It must also be said that Luther was often unfair to the monasteries. Many monks and nuns had given themselves to prayer and service in genuine faith, not in hope of earning heaven. And later Protestant cultures have sometimes turned his teaching into something he would not have recognised: a worship of work and productivity, as if busy-ness were holiness. Luther was not a workaholic. He believed in rest, in feasting, in the Sabbath, and in the God who gives to His beloved even in their sleep.

FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Write down the callings God has given you — in family, work, church and community — and thank Him for each by name.

2. Choose one ordinary task you do tomorrow and ask, “Whom does this serve?” Then do it for that person, as to the Lord.

3. If you have thought your work unspiritual, read Psalm 145:15–16 and ask how God is feeding His world through you.

4. Identify the cross in your present calling. Ask for patience to bear it rather than escape it.

5. If your calling has become an idol of busy-ness, set aside real rest this week as an act of trust.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You feed and clothe and protect Your world, and You have chosen to do it through human hands.
Thank You for the callings You have given me, in my home, my work and my neighbourhood.
Let me do what my hand finds to do heartily, as to You, and for the good of those You have put near me.
When my work is hard, give me patience; when it is ordinary, let me see Your hand behind it; and when it is done, give me rest in You. Amen.
