fields.body_html:
For as many of you as have been baptized into Christ have put on Christ. GALATIANS 3:27

There is a story, told of Luther in his seasons of dark temptation, that when the devil pressed hardest on him with accusations he did not argue about his feelings or his works. He simply answered, I am baptised. Some say he chalked the words on his table. Whether or not the details are exact, the story is true to the man. For Luther, baptism was not a quaint ceremony performed on babies and then forgotten. It was the solid ground under his feet, the one fact about himself that no temptation could shake, because it was not his work but God’s.

Water with the Word

In his Small Catechism of 1529, Luther asked the simplest questions about baptism and gave the simplest answers. What is baptism? It is not plain water only, but water used according to God’s command and joined with God’s Word. What does it give? It works forgiveness of sins, delivers from death and the devil, and gives eternal salvation to all who believe, as the words and promises of God declare. How can water do such great things? It is not the water, Luther answers, but the Word of God with the water, and faith that trusts that Word.

He that believeth and is baptized shall be saved; but he that believeth not shall be damned. MARK 16:16

This was typical of Luther’s whole approach to the sacraments. Everything depends on the promise. In On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church, written in 1520, he complained that the medieval church had surrounded baptism with ceremonies and then taught people that, after it, they must be saved by penance, as though baptism were a ship that had been wrecked by sin and they must now swim to shore on a plank. No, said Luther. The ship does not sink. The promise God made in baptism stands for life. When we fall, we return not to a plank but to the ship: to our baptism, and to the God who made His promise there.

Go ye therefore, and teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Ghost. MATTHEW 28:19

A daily drowning

Baptism is not only a past event. Luther taught that it signifies a daily dying and rising. In the catechism he explains that the old Adam in us should be drowned by daily sorrow and repentance and die with all sins and evil desires, and that a new person should daily come forth and rise to live before God in righteousness and purity for ever. The Christian life is a return to baptism every morning.

Know ye not, that so many of us as were baptized into Jesus Christ were baptized into his death? Therefore we are buried with him by baptism into death: that like as Christ was raised up from the dead by the glory of the Father, even so we also should walk in newness of life. ROMANS 6:3–4

His sermon on how to contemplate Christ’s sufferings touches the same truth from another angle. He says that true meditation on the cross, even for a quarter of an hour, does more than a year of fasting, because it kills the old self and gives new life:

“For such a meditation changes a man’s character and almost as in baptism he is born again, anew.”

The old Adam, Luther liked to say, is a strong swimmer. He must be drowned again and again. But the promise of baptism means that the new life is already ours, and the drowning is not a hopeless struggle but a following of what God has already done.

Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost. TITUS 3:5

The baptism of infants

Luther defended the baptism of infants firmly, both against Rome’s later additions and against the Anabaptists, who taught that only believers able to confess their faith should be baptised. His argument rested again on the Word. Baptism is God’s work, not ours; it rests on His command and promise, not on the strength of our faith. We do not baptise because we are sure the child believes, he said, but because God commands it and promises to work through it. And he pointed to Christ’s welcome of the little ones.

But when Jesus saw it, he was much displeased, and said unto them, Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God. MARK 10:14
For the promise is unto you, and to your children, and to all that are afar off, even as many as the Lord our God shall call. ACTS 2:39

Where Christians differ

It must be said fairly that faithful Christians disagree with Luther here. Baptists and many others believe that baptism should follow a personal confession of faith, and that the New Testament pattern is of believers being baptised. Reformed Christians share Luther’s practice of infant baptism but speak more cautiously of what baptism does, calling it a sign and seal rather than the means that gives salvation. Luther himself insisted that baptism without faith profits nothing; he did not teach that the water works like magic. But he spoke of baptism’s power more strongly than many of his fellow Protestants could, and readers must weigh his words against Scripture.

A darker matter also belongs here. Luther’s disagreement with the Anabaptists was not only theological. In the 1530s he joined his colleagues in approving the death penalty for Anabaptists judged to be seditious or blasphemous, and many were executed in Protestant as well as Catholic lands. Many Lutherans today have formally sought forgiveness from the Mennonite churches for this history. It is a sober reminder that right teaching about the sacrament of grace did not always produce grace towards those who disagreed.

The like figure whereunto even baptism doth also now save us (not the putting away of the filth of the flesh, but the answer of a good conscience toward God,) by the resurrection of Jesus Christ. 1 PETER 3:21

Standing on the promise

Whatever view the reader takes of the time and mode of baptism, Luther’s central insight belongs to every Christian. Our assurance does not rest on our feelings, our progress or the strength of our faith. It rests on the promise God has spoken and sealed to us. When the accuser comes, we do not point to ourselves. We point to what God has done. In the moment of temptation, the most powerful words are not I feel or I have done but God has said. For Luther, baptism was God’s saying it, with water, over him by name.

1. Find out, if you can, the date of your baptism. Give thanks for it this year as you would for a birthday.

2. The next time you are accused by your conscience, answer as Luther did, pointing not to your feelings but to God’s promise in Christ.

3. Begin each day this week with a short prayer of dying and rising: “Lord, let the old self die today, and let me live to You.”

4. If you hold a different view of baptism from Luther’s, read Romans 6 and ask what you can learn from him about the promise even where you differ.

5. Pray for Christians of other traditions whom your own tradition has wronged, and for reconciliation.

Father, Son and Holy Spirit, into whose name I have been baptised, thank You for the promise You have made to me.
When my sins accuse me and my feelings fail, let me rest on what You have said and done.
Drown in me today the old self with all its evil desires, and raise me to walk in newness of life.
Keep me in the grace of my baptism until the day I rise with Christ, and make me gentle towards all who bear His name. Amen.

fields.title: This Is My Body
fields.body_html:
And he took bread, and gave thanks, and brake it, and gave unto them, saying, This is my body which is given for you: this do in remembrance of me. LUKE 22:19

No subject caused Luther more grief, or brought out more of his stubbornness, than the Lord’s Supper. It divided him first from Rome and then, more painfully, from fellow Reformers who agreed with him on almost everything else. Readers who come from other traditions will find some of what follows hard to accept, and they should know at the outset that this chapter describes a place where sincere Christians have disagreed for five hundred years. But it is impossible to understand Luther without understanding why this mattered to him so much. For him, the Supper was the gospel in bread and wine, and the heart of it was two words: for you.

Against the captivity

In 1520 Luther wrote On the Babylonian Captivity of the Church, the most radical of his treatises that year. In it he argued that the Supper had been held captive in three ways. First, the cup had been withheld from the laity, though Christ said, Drink ye all of it. Second, the church had bound consciences to the philosophical theory of transubstantiation, which explained how the bread became Christ’s body in the language of Aristotle; Luther believed that Christ was truly present, but thought no one should be forced to accept a particular explanation of how. Third, and worst, the Mass had been turned into a sacrifice offered by the priest to God, a good work performed for the living and the dead, and sold for money.

That third captivity struck at the gospel itself. The Supper, Luther said, is not something we offer to God. It is something God gives to us: a testament, a promise sealed by Christ’s death, handing us the forgiveness of sins. To turn it into our work was to turn the gift upside down.

For by one offering he hath perfected for ever them that are sanctified. HEBREWS 10:14

His early sermon on Christ’s sufferings had already made the point sharply. Those who think it is enough simply to attend Mass, as if the ceremony worked by itself, miss its purpose, which is to bring the sufferings of Christ home to us. He asks:

“For what help is it to you, that God is God, if he is not God to you?”

Given for you

In the Small Catechism, Luther explains the Supper with the same simplicity he used for baptism. It is the true body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, under the bread and wine, given for Christians to eat and drink, instituted by Christ Himself. What does it give? The words tell us: given and shed for you for the forgiveness of sins. And where there is forgiveness of sins, Luther adds, there is also life and salvation. Who receives it worthily? The one who believes those words, for you.

For this is my blood of the new testament, which is shed for many for the remission of sins. MATTHEW 26:28

The Supper, then, is not first a memorial of an absent Christ, nor a proof of our devotion, but a meal in which the present Christ gives Himself and His forgiveness to sinners. Luther urged troubled believers to come often, precisely because they were troubled. The Supper was medicine for the sick, not a reward for the healthy.

The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not the communion of the blood of Christ? The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ? 1 CORINTHIANS 10:16

Marburg

In the 1520s Luther found himself facing Reformers who read the words This is my body differently. Ulrich Zwingli of Zurich, and others with him, argued that is here means signifies, as when Christ says I am the door. The bread represents Christ’s body; the Supper is a memorial and a pledge of faith. Christ’s body, they argued, is in heaven at the right hand of God and cannot be in many places at once.

Luther would not accept it. The words say is, he insisted, and we have no right to change them. Christ, who is God, can be present as He wills; the right hand of God is not a place in the sky but God’s power, which is everywhere. In October 1529 the Landgrave Philip of Hesse brought the two sides together at his castle at Marburg, hoping to unite the Protestants against their enemies. Luther is said to have chalked the words This is my body on the table before him and refused to move from them. The theologians agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles of faith. On one point within the last article, the bodily presence of Christ in the bread, they could not agree, and they parted without fellowship at the Lord’s Table.

Take, eat; this is my body. MATTHEW 26:26

A fair judgement

What are we to make of this? Three things can be said with some confidence. First, Luther was right that the Supper is Christ’s gift before it is our act, and that its heart is the forgiveness of sins. Christians of every view can learn from that. Second, his opponents were not despisers of the sacrament. Zwingli loved Christ and sought faithfully to honour His words, and John Calvin, a little later, taught a real spiritual feeding on Christ in the Supper that stands between the two positions. Third, Luther’s refusal to acknowledge Zwingli and his friends as brothers in Christ, and the harsh language he used about them, did lasting harm. The division of the Protestant churches over the table where Christ prayed for His people to be one is a sorrow, and Luther’s temper made it worse.

Endeavouring to keep the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. EPHESIANS 4:3

The reader who shares Luther’s view will find in his writings a deep and consoling theology of Christ’s nearness. The reader who does not will still find in him a man who took Christ’s words with utter seriousness, and who could not bear to see them softened. Both may learn humility from Marburg.

Coming to the table

However we understand the manner of Christ’s presence, Luther’s pastoral counsel holds. Come to the Supper as a beggar, not as a saint. Examine yourself, not to find whether you are worthy, but to find whether you need forgiveness, and if you do, come. Listen to the words for you, and believe them. And go from the table to love your neighbour, for, as Luther often said, the Supper makes us one loaf with Christ and with each other.

But let a man examine himself, and so let him eat of that bread, and drink of that cup. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:28
For as often as ye eat this bread, and drink this cup, ye do shew the Lord’s death till he come. 1 CORINTHIANS 11:26
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. The next time you come to the Lord’s Table, listen for the words for you and receive them personally.

2. If you have stayed away from the Supper because you felt unworthy, consider Luther’s counsel that it is medicine for the sick, and speak to your pastor.

3. Learn the view of the Supper held by a Christian tradition other than your own, from its own writers, and pray for its members.

4. Ask whether there is a fellow Christian with whom you have refused fellowship over a secondary matter. Seek to be reconciled as far as conscience allows.

5. After receiving the Supper, look for a practical way to serve someone who shares the same table.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, on the night You were betrayed You gave Your disciples bread and wine, and said, This is my body, given for you.
Thank You that at Your table You give and do not demand, and that there You hand me the forgiveness of my sins.
Forgive Your church for the bitterness with which we have argued over Your gift, and make us one as You and the Father are one.
Feed me with Yourself, and send me out to love my neighbour, until You come. Amen.

fields.title: A Simple Way to Pray
fields.body_html:
After this manner therefore pray ye: Our Father which art in heaven, Hallowed be thy name. MATTHEW 6:9

In 1535 Luther’s barber, a master named Peter Beskendorf, asked him how to pray. It was a simple question from an ordinary man, and the busiest theologian in Europe answered it with a little book. A Simple Way to Pray, addressed to him as a good friend, is one of the most practical things Luther ever wrote, and one of the most revealing. It shows how the great Reformer actually prayed, day by day, when he was not preaching or fighting. It is also full of humour and humility. Luther confesses that he, too, has days when he is cold and unwilling to pray, and he tells Peter what he does about it.

Warming the heart

When he felt his heart growing cool and distracted, Luther said, he would take his little psalter, go to his room or, if it was a church day, to church among the people, and begin to say the Ten Commandments, the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to himself, word by word, as he had done since childhood, and perhaps some words of Christ or Paul or the Psalms. He did not wait to feel like praying. He used the words he knew to warm his heart until it was ready. Prayer, for Luther, was not the fruit of a good mood; it was the remedy for a bad one.

He urged Peter to make prayer the first business of the morning and the last of the night, and to guard against the thought that he would pray in an hour when he had finished this or that. Such thoughts, he warned, lead away from prayer altogether, and the day is lost.

My voice shalt thou hear in the morning, O LORD; in the morning will I direct my prayer unto thee, and will look up. PSALM 5:3

A garland of four strands

Luther’s method was to take a familiar text — a petition of the Lord’s Prayer, one of the commandments, an article of the Creed — and to make of it a garland of four strands. First, he asked what it teaches: what God is saying to me here. Second, he gave thanks for it. Third, he confessed the sin it shows me. Fourth, he prayed for help. fields.title: The Catechism at the Kitchen Table
fields.body_html:
And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children. DEUTERONOMY 6:6–7

In 1528 Luther joined in a visitation of the parishes of Electoral Saxony, travelling from village to village to see how the churches were faring now that the old order had collapsed. What he found appalled him. In the preface to his Small Catechism he describes it: ordinary people, especially in the villages, knew almost nothing of the Christian faith, and many pastors were quite unable to teach it. People could not say the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed or the Ten Commandments. They had been baptised and took the sacrament, yet lived, he says in effect, like cattle, and now that the gospel had come, many had learned only to abuse their freedom. Luther did not write a denunciation. He wrote a handbook.

Two catechisms

In 1529 he published two catechisms. The Large Catechism was for pastors and preachers, a full, vigorous explanation of the faith in plain German, based on sermons he had preached. The Small Catechism was for the household. It was printed first as wall charts to hang up in the home, and its questions and answers were designed for the head of the family to teach to children and servants. Its heart is five parts: the Ten Commandments, the Apostles’ Creed, the Lord’s Prayer, baptism and the Lord’s Supper, with a section on confession, prayers for morning and evening, graces before and after meals, and a table of duties for different callings.

Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it. PROVERBS 22:6

The order is deliberate. First the commandments, which show us our sin and our need. Then the Creed, which shows us the God who meets that need — Father, Son and Holy Spirit. Then the Lord’s Prayer, which teaches us to ask for what we need. Then the sacraments, through which God gives it. Law, gospel, prayer, and the means of grace: the whole Christian life on a few pages.

A faith for the whole household

The Small Catechism is famous for the question it asks again and again: What does this mean? Each commandment, each article of the Creed and each petition of the Lord’s Prayer is followed by that simple question, and a short, memorable answer. The first commandment, Luther explains, means that we should fear, love and trust God above all things; and every commandment after it begins with the same words, we should fear and love God. Obedience flows from a relationship, not a rulebook.

His explanation of the second article of the Creed is often called the finest paragraph he ever wrote. In it the child confesses that Jesus Christ, true God and true man, is my Lord, who has redeemed me, a lost and condemned person, not with gold or silver but with His holy, precious blood and His innocent suffering and death, that I may be His own and live under Him in His kingdom and serve Him in everlasting righteousness, innocence and blessedness. It is the whole gospel, told in the first person, simple enough for a child and deep enough for a lifetime.

Forasmuch as ye know that ye were not redeemed with corruptible things, as silver and gold, from your vain conversation received by tradition from your fathers; but with the precious blood of Christ, as of a lamb without blemish and without spot. 1 PETER 1:18–19

In the Large Catechism, explaining the first commandment, he gives a definition that has become well known: whatever your heart clings to and relies upon, that is really your god. It is a searching test. Every one of us has something we trust for security, meaning and comfort. The catechism asks whether it is God.

The doctor who stayed a pupil

Luther did not think the catechism was only for children. In the preface to the Large Catechism he tells pastors who think it beneath them that he himself, a doctor of theology, still recites it daily, word by word, like a child, and remains a pupil of it gladly. Those who imagine they have mastered it, he says, have not begun to understand it.

His sermon on the appearing of the grace of God makes a similar point. Commenting on Paul’s word that grace teaches us, he notes that it is the word used for the elementary teaching given to children, and says:

“God designs that we, as childish pupils, be instructed by his saving grace.”

Verily I say unto you, Except ye be converted, and become as little children, ye shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven. MATTHEW 18:3

In the same sermon he says that the work of a minister is twofold, teaching and exhortation: “We must teach the uninformed, and must admonish the already informed lest they go backward, grow indolent or fall away entirely instead of persevering against all temptations.” The catechism served both. It taught the ignorant, and it kept reminding the rest.

At the kitchen table

The genius of the Small Catechism was to put the teaching of the faith back where Scripture puts it: in the home. Luther did not think faith could be left to the professionals. The father and mother were to be the first pastors of their children, teaching them the commandments, the Creed and the Prayer at table and at bedtime, praying with them morning and evening, asking the simple question, What does this mean?

And, ye fathers, provoke not your children to wrath: but bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord. EPHESIANS 6:4
That the generation to come might know them, even the children which should be born; who should arise and declare them to their children. PSALM 78:6

Honest cautions

Every good tool can be misused. In later generations, catechism teaching in some Lutheran lands became dry and mechanical: children learned the answers by heart, recited them for the pastor, and forgot them. The Pietists of the following century rightly complained that head knowledge had sometimes replaced living faith. Luther would have agreed with them. He wanted the words learned so that they could be prayed and lived, not merely repeated.

It is also true that the table of duties in the Small Catechism assumes the social order of sixteenth-century Saxony, with its masters and servants. Its Scriptures remain true, but readers will apply them wisely to a very different world.

None of this diminishes the gift. Few books have done more good, in more homes, over more centuries, than that little catechism written in response to the ignorance of Saxon villages.

Hold fast the form of sound words, which thou hast heard of me, in faith and love which is in Christ Jesus. 2 TIMOTHY 1:13
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Can you say the Ten Commandments, the Apostles’ Creed and the Lord’s Prayer from memory? If not, learn whichever you lack this month.

2. Take one line of the Creed each day this week and ask Luther’s question: What does this mean — for me?

3. Apply the Large Catechism’s test: what does your heart cling to and rely upon? Name it honestly before God.

4. If you have children or others in your care, choose a simple time each day to pray and teach the faith with them at home.

5. Read Luther’s explanation of the second article of the Creed slowly, and make it your own confession of faith.

A PRAYER
Lord God, You have given us Your commandments, Your promises and Your prayer, and You have commanded us to teach them to our children.
Forgive me where I have left the teaching of the faith to others, and where I have thought myself too grown-up to be taught.
Make me a humble pupil of Your grace all my days, and let my home be a place where Your Word is spoken and prayed.
I believe that Jesus Christ is my Lord, who has redeemed me; let me be His own, and live under Him, and serve Him for ever. Amen.

fields.title: Anfechtung: The Assaults of the Soul
fields.body_html:
Why art thou cast down, O my soul? and why art thou disquieted within me? hope thou in God: for I shall yet praise him, who is the health of my countenance, and my God. PSALM 42:11

There is a German word that runs all through Luther’s life and writing, and it has no single English equivalent. Anfechtung means, roughly, an assault or attack; it is often translated temptation, trial or spiritual struggle. But for Luther it meant something deeper than being tempted to sin. It meant the experience of feeling abandoned by God, accused by the law, terrified by death and judgement, and unable to find comfort anywhere. It was the darkness he had known as a young friar, and it did not leave him when he discovered the gospel. It came back again and again, sometimes for weeks together, until the end of his life.

A man acquainted with darkness

Luther was not a serene saint who had risen above struggle. At the Wartburg in 1521 he was ill, sleepless and assailed by doubts about whether he had done right to divide the church. In 1527 he suffered a collapse, with fainting and a terrible sense of God’s absence, and wrote to friends asking for their prayers. In that same year plague came to Wittenberg; the university moved away, but Luther stayed with his pregnant wife to care for the sick. He knew what it was to believe the gospel with his mind while his heart felt only accusation.

LORD, why castest thou off my soul? why hidest thou thy face from me? PSALM 88:14

Strikingly, he came to believe that these assaults were not signs that his faith had failed, but part of how God makes a Christian. In a preface he wrote in 1539 to his German writings, he said that three things make a theologian: prayer, meditation on the Word, and Anfechtung. It is trial, he said, that teaches us not only to know and understand but to experience how true, how sweet, how mighty and how comforting God’s Word is. Without it, the Christian knows the gospel only as words.

Feeling and faith

The heart of Luther’s counsel in times of spiritual darkness was to distinguish between feeling and faith. His Easter sermon on the resurrection deals with a question every troubled Christian asks: if Christ has conquered sin and death, why do I still feel them in me? Luther answers:

“I have often said before that feeling and faith are two different things.”

He goes on to explain that faith clings to the Word even when feeling contradicts it. We must, he says, accept only the Word and write it into our hearts, even when it seems as if our sins were not taken from us. Feelings rise and fall like waves on the sea; the Word stands like the shore. The waves, he says, strive against us as though they would destroy us, but in the end they must grow weary and fall back.

Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief. MARK 9:24
Who is among you that feareth the LORD, that obeyeth the voice of his servant, that walketh in darkness, and hath no light? let him trust in the name of the LORD, and stay upon his God. ISAIAH 50:10

Peace in the storm

Luther’s Pentecost sermon offers another comfort. The peace Christ gives, he says, is not the peace the world gives. The world thinks peace is the removal of trouble. Christ often leaves the trouble where it is. Instead, Luther says, “he changes the heart, removing it from the affliction, not the affliction from the heart.”

He adds that the Holy Spirit’s work in us is never finished in this life, and that we must not conclude He has abandoned us because we still feel fear. The Spirit’s office, he says, continues as long as we live, “in such manner that sorrow is ever mingled with peace.” Indeed, he adds, if there were no sorrow, the Spirit could not comfort us.

Peace I leave with you, my peace I give unto you: not as the world giveth, give I unto you. Let not your heart be troubled, neither let it be afraid. JOHN 14:27

Christ in the darkness

Above all, Luther pointed the tempted to Christ, who Himself cried out on the cross that God had forsaken Him. Our darkness is not a place Christ has never been. He entered the deepest abandonment so that no believer would ever be truly abandoned. When we feel forsaken, we are in His company, and He has passed through to the resurrection.

And about the ninth hour Jesus cried with a loud voice, saying, Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani? that is to say, My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? MATTHEW 27:46

Practical counsel

Luther’s letters to troubled friends are full of practical wisdom. He told the melancholy not to be alone, for the devil loves solitude; to seek good company, talk, music, even a joke; to eat and drink and rest; not to argue with the tempter about their sins, but to point him to Christ. He urged them to sing, to recite the Creed, and to lean on the prayers of others. To one young man, a tutor in his household troubled by gloomy thoughts, he wrote urging him to drive the devil away with cheerfulness and company rather than to brood.

We are troubled on every side, yet not distressed; we are perplexed, but not in despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; cast down, but not destroyed. 2 CORINTHIANS 4:8–9

A caution

It must be said that Luther saw the devil’s hand in almost all such darkness, and not every modern reader will follow him there. Some of what he suffered may well have been illness of body or mind, which today would be treated by a physician. fields.title: A Mighty Fortress
fields.body_html:
God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. PSALM 46:1

Luther loved music with a passion that surprised even his friends. He played the lute and sang in a good tenor voice; as a schoolboy in Eisenach he had sung in the streets for bread. He composed melodies, wrote hymns, and gathered singers around his table in the evenings. In a letter of 1530 to the composer Ludwig Senfl he is remembered as saying that, after theology, he gave music the highest place and the greatest honour. For a man who thought theology the queen of the sciences, that was praise indeed.

Why music matters

Luther believed that music is a gift of God, not an invention of human beings. It belongs to creation; the birds sing, and even the air, moved and struck, makes sound. But it becomes most glorious when it carries the Word of God. Music, he thought, has a unique power to move the heart, to comfort the sad, to calm the anxious, and to drive away the devil, who cannot bear the sound of joyful praise. He liked to point to David playing his harp before the troubled king.

And it came to pass, when the evil spirit from God was upon Saul, that David took an harp, and played with his hand: so Saul was refreshed, and was well, and the evil spirit departed from him. 1 SAMUEL 16:23

This was not merely a matter of taste. It came from his theology of the Word. If the Word of God is living and powerful, then anything that carries that Word into the heart and memory is precious. Music does that better than almost anything else. A sermon may be forgotten by Tuesday; a hymn sung on Sunday is still being hummed in the kitchen on Saturday.

Let the word of Christ dwell in you richly in all wisdom; teaching and admonishing one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with grace in your hearts to the Lord. COLOSSIANS 3:16

The people’s song

In the medieval church, the congregation mostly listened while the choir and clergy sang in Latin. Luther wanted the people to sing, in their own language, the gospel they were learning. From 1523 he began writing hymns in German and encouraging friends to do the same. The first songs appeared in small printed collections in 1524, and soon whole hymnbooks followed. He worked closely with the musician Johann Walter to set the new texts.

His very first song was not a hymn at all but a ballad. In 1523 two young Augustinian friars, followers of Luther’s teaching, were burned for heresy in Brussels. Luther wrote a song about them, telling their story and praising God for their faithfulness. It shows how closely, for him, singing and suffering belonged together.

Many of his hymns are paraphrases of Scripture. Out of the depths I cry to Thee sets the hundred and thirtieth Psalm, and became one of the best-loved funeral hymns in Germany. For Christmas, around 1535, he wrote a long carol, From heaven above to earth I come, for his own family to sing, with an angel announcing the birth and the children answering.

Out of the depths have I cried unto thee, O LORD. PSALM 130:1

The angels’ song

Luther’s Christmas sermon on the birth of Jesus spends a long time on the song of the angels, Glory to God in the highest. He sees in it the whole shape of the Christian heart: giving all glory to God, living at peace with others, and taking pleasure in all that God does. And he gives a lovely picture of what true praise looks like:

“Therefore if you would think of a humble, pure, obedient and joyful heart, praising God, think of the angels.”

And suddenly there was with the angel a multitude of the heavenly host praising God, and saying, Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will toward men. LUKE 2:13–14

A mighty fortress

The most famous of all Luther’s hymns was written in the late 1520s, in a time of great danger. The Reformation faced hostility from the Emperor, and plague and the threat of Turkish invasion hung over Europe. Luther turned to the forty-sixth Psalm and wrote Ein feste Burg ist unser Gott — A mighty fortress is our God. It is not a gentle hymn. It is a battle song. It names the old evil foe with his craft and power, admits that our own strength is nothing, and then points to the one who fights for us, Jesus Christ, the Lord of hosts. It ends in defiance: let them take everything, even life itself; the kingdom remains ours.

Therefore will not we fear, though the earth be removed, and though the mountains be carried into the midst of the sea. PSALM 46:2
Be still, and know that I am God: I will be exalted among the heathen, I will be exalted in the earth. PSALM 46:10

The hymn became the anthem of the Reformation. It has been sung at coronations and funerals, in prisons and on battlefields, and translated into scores of languages. It carries in a few verses almost the whole of Luther’s faith: the reality of the devil, the weakness of man, the victory of Christ, and the unshakeable Word.

Honest notes

Two notes of caution belong here. First, Luther’s love of music in worship was balanced by a principle he stated clearly in his sermon on the appearing of the grace of God: that none of the outward trappings of worship are necessary, not even organs and singing, and that “The Gospel is the true bell, the true organ, for divine service.” He did not make music a law. Other Reformers, such as Zwingli in Zurich, removed organs and choirs altogether; Luther kept them because they served the Word, not because they were required.

Second, A mighty fortress has not always been sung in its own spirit. In later centuries it was sometimes turned into a song of German national pride, even of war, as though the fortress were the nation rather than God. Luther wrote it for a frightened church trusting in Christ, not for an army trusting in itself.

And at midnight Paul and Silas prayed, and sang praises unto God: and the prisoners heard them. ACTS 16:25
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Learn by heart one hymn that carries the gospel clearly, and sing it when you are anxious or tempted.

2. Read Psalm 46 each day this week, and then sing or read the words of A mighty fortress.

3. If you have children, sing with them at home — at meals, at bedtime, at festivals — as Luther did with his.

4. In church this Sunday, sing the words as a confession of faith, not merely a tune.

5. When you feel low, try Luther’s remedy: put on or sing music that carries God’s Word, and let it lift your heart.

A PRAYER
Lord of hosts, You are our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
Thank You for the gift of music, and for every song that carries Your Word into our hearts and homes.
When fear comes, let me sing of Your faithfulness; when the enemy accuses, let me sing of Christ who fights for me.
Give me a humble, pure, obedient and joyful heart, praising You with the angels, now and for ever. Amen.

fields.title: My Lord Katie
fields.body_html:
And the LORD God said, It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him. GENESIS 2:18

On Easter Eve 1523 a group of nuns escaped from the Cistercian convent of Nimbschen, near Grimma in Saxony, hidden, as the story goes, in a merchant’s wagon among empty herring barrels. They had read Luther’s writings and wanted to leave the cloister, and he had helped arrange their escape. Several were brought to Wittenberg, and Luther set about finding them husbands or homes. One of them, Katharina von Bora, a spirited woman of twenty-four from an impoverished noble family, turned down the match proposed for her and let it be known that she would marry Luther himself, or his friend Nicholas von Amsdorf. On 13 June 1525 she married Luther. He was forty-one.

Marriage restored

Luther had been writing about marriage long before he married. In The Estate of Marriage, published in 1522, he argued that marriage is a holy order established by God at creation, not a lesser state for those too weak for celibacy. The medieval church had exalted the vowed celibate life above marriage, forbidden priests to marry, and treated sexual desire with deep suspicion. Luther believed this had done great harm. God made us male and female, and blessed marriage before the fall. To despise it is to despise His work.

Marriage is honourable in all, and the bed undefiled: but whoremongers and adulterers God will judge. HEBREWS 13:4

He did not think marriage was a sacrament in the sense of a means of saving grace; it belonged to the order of creation, shared by Christians and unbelievers alike. But he thought it one of God’s richest gifts and one of the most demanding callings. It is a school of love, of patience, of forgiveness, and of the daily cross.

Now the Spirit speaketh expressly, that in the latter times some shall depart from the faith … forbidding to marry, and commanding to abstain from meats, which God hath created to be received with thanksgiving. 1 TIMOTHY 4:1–3

His Christmas sermon on the birth of Jesus shows how deeply he honoured ordinary human life. He insists that Mary’s childbirth was a real birth, like any other mother’s, and that she nursed her child as any mother does. He draws a principle from it:

“Grace does not interfere with nature and her work, but rather improves and promotes it.”

A little later he adds: “It is a great comfort to us that Jesus took upon himself our nature and flesh.” The body, sex, childbirth and family life are not unholy things that grace must escape. They are good creations that grace comes to heal.

The Black Cloister

The Luthers lived in the old Augustinian house in Wittenberg, given to them by the Elector. Katharina ran it with remarkable energy. She managed farms, gardens, fishponds and livestock, brewed beer, took in student boarders, nursed the sick, and fed a household that often numbered dozens. Luther called her, teasingly, my lord Katie, and he made fun of himself for being ruled by her. His letters to her are full of affection and jokes, and he once said that he would not exchange her for France and Venice together.

Who can find a virtuous woman? for her price is far above rubies. PROVERBS 31:10

They had six children. Their daughter Elizabeth died before her first birthday. Their beloved Magdalena died in 1542, aged thirteen. Luther’s grief was enormous. He knelt by her bed and prayed that God would spare her, and then, when it was clear she was dying, told God he would gladly leave her with Him. Those who were there recorded his words: that she was well provided for, and yet the parting grieved him beyond measure. The great teacher of the resurrection wept like any father.

Lo, children are an heritage of the LORD: and the fruit of the womb is his reward. PSALM 127:3
But I would not have you to be ignorant, brethren, concerning them which are asleep, that ye sorrow not, even as others which have no hope. 1 THESSALONIANS 4:13

A marriage that taught the Reformation

The Luthers’ household became a model for Protestant family life for centuries. The pastor’s home — husband, wife, children, guests, students, prayer at table, the catechism taught at the fireside — became a fixture of European Christianity. It showed that holiness could be lived out in the kitchen and the nursery, and that a Christian woman could be a partner in ministry without taking a vow.

When Luther made his will in 1542, he left everything to Katharina, against the custom of the time, which gave a widow’s property into the hands of male guardians. He wrote that she had been a pious and faithful wife who had loved him dearly. It was an act of trust and honour unusual for its age.

Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it. EPHESIANS 5:25

Honest cautions

There are shadows here too. Luther’s words about women were sometimes coarse and patronising, shaped by the assumptions of his time, and some of them are hard to read today. His teaching on the order of the household assumed a strong authority for the husband and father that can be, and has been, abused.

More seriously, in 1539 Luther and Melanchthon gave secret advice to Philip of Hesse, a leading Protestant prince, that he might take a second wife while the first still lived, rather than live in adultery, provided it was kept quiet. When the bigamy became known, it caused scandal and harmed the Reformation. Luther’s counsel was a grave error, contrary to the teaching of Christ on marriage, and born partly of political pressure. It is a warning that even the best teachers can bend the Word for the powerful.

After Luther’s death, Katharina struggled. War drove her from Wittenberg, the household fell into debt, and in 1552, fleeing plague, she was injured in an accident on the road and died at Torgau some weeks later. The woman who had held together the Reformer’s home deserves to be remembered in her own right.

Thy wife shall be as a fruitful vine by the sides of thine house: thy children like olive plants round about thy table. PSALM 128:3
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. If you are married, thank God for your spouse this week in words spoken to them, as Luther did in his letters to Katie.

2. If you are single, thank God that your life is not lesser in His sight, and ask how your household can be a place of welcome.

3. Consider where you have treated the body, family life or ordinary love as less holy than religious activity. Receive them again as God’s gifts.

4. If you are grieving a child or someone dear, bring your grief to God honestly, as Luther did, and let others share it with you.

5. Ask whether you have ever bent God’s Word to please someone powerful. Repent, and resolve to speak plainly.

A PRAYER
Creator God, You made us male and female, and You have blessed marriage and family as Your good gifts.
Thank You for the homes in which we have been loved, and forgive us where we have failed those closest to us.
Let grace heal and perfect our nature, and let our households be places of prayer, welcome and joy.
Comfort all who grieve for children and loved ones, and keep us in the hope of the resurrection, through Jesus Christ, who took our flesh. Amen.

fields.title: Two Kingdoms
fields.body_html:
Then saith he unto them, Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s. MATTHEW 22:21

Luther lived in a world where church and state were tangled together in every possible way. Bishops were princes, princes appointed bishops, the pope claimed authority over emperors, and heresy was a crime punished by fire. When the Reformation broke that world apart, a question pressed urgently on everyone: what is the proper work of the ruler, and what is the proper work of the church? Luther’s answer, worked out especially in a treatise of 1523 on temporal authority and how far it should be obeyed, is usually called the doctrine of the two kingdoms. It is one of his most influential teachings, and one of the most debated.

Two ways God rules

Luther taught that God rules the world in two ways. In His spiritual kingdom, He rules the hearts of believers by His Word and Spirit, through the preaching of the gospel. There is no compulsion here: faith cannot be forced, and the only weapon is the Word. In His temporal kingdom, God rules the whole world, believers and unbelievers alike, through law, government and the sword, to restrain evil and keep outward peace. Both are God’s. Both are good. But they must not be confused.

Jesus answered, My kingdom is not of this world: if my kingdom were of this world, then would my servants fight. JOHN 18:36

Luther saw a sign of this in the very circumstances of Christ’s birth. In his Christmas sermon he notes that Jesus was born at the time of Caesar Augustus’s census, and draws the lesson:

“By this Jesus shows that his kingdom was not to be of an earthly character nor to exercise worldly power and lordship, but that he, together with his parents, is subject to the powers that be.”

Why the sword is needed

If everyone were a true Christian, Luther reasoned, there would be no need for courts, police or armies. Christians, moved by the Spirit, would do right without being forced. But true Christians are few, and even they remain sinners. So God has ordained government to protect the innocent and punish the wicked. His Pentecost sermon states the principle bluntly: Christians, ruled by the Spirit, do not need the law’s compulsion, but “Those, however, who are not Christians must be controlled by laws, and be subjected to executioners and governed by the sword, in order that they be compelled not to do evil with the hand.”

Let every soul be subject unto the higher powers. For there is no power but of God: the powers that be are ordained of God. ROMANS 13:1
For he beareth not the sword in vain: for he is the minister of God, a revenger to execute wrath upon him that doeth evil. ROMANS 13:4

This means that a Christian may serve as a magistrate, a judge or a soldier, as a calling from God and a work of love for the neighbour. For himself, the Christian turns the other cheek and bears injustice patiently. For his neighbour, he may take up the office of the sword to protect the weak.

But I say unto you, That ye resist not evil: but whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also. MATTHEW 5:39

The limits of rulers

The other half of the teaching was a check on rulers. Temporal government, Luther insisted, has authority only over bodies and goods, over outward things. It has no authority over souls. No prince may command what people believe, and heresy, he wrote in 1523, cannot be driven out by force but only by the Word of God. When rulers command what God forbids, or try to rule consciences, Christians must refuse, suffering the consequences rather than obeying.

Then Peter and the other apostles answered and said, We ought to obey God rather than men. ACTS 5:29

He also rebuked rulers for tyranny. In the spring of 1525, as the peasants of southern and central Germany rose against their lords, Luther wrote an Admonition to Peace. He told the princes plainly that they had brought the revolt on themselves by their greed and oppression, and he told the peasants that rebellion was not the way of the gospel. Both sides, he said, were in the wrong.

The Peasants’ War

Then the revolt turned violent, and Luther’s tone changed completely. Within weeks he published a short tract against the robbing and murdering hordes of peasants, urging the princes to strike them down without mercy, to stab and slay as one would a mad dog. It was published as the rulers were already crushing the rebellion, and in the battle of Frankenhausen and elsewhere many thousands of peasants were killed. When he was criticised, Luther defended himself and did not withdraw his words.

This must be said plainly: it was a terrible thing to write. Whatever the wrongs of the rebels, a pastor and teacher of the gospel called for the slaughter of poor men with language no Christian should use, and gave the powerful a warrant for cruelty. It cost him the trust of many of the common people, and it is hard to blame them.

He hath shewed thee, O man, what is good; and what doth the LORD require of thee, but to do justly, and to love mercy, and to walk humbly with thy God? MICAH 6:8

A teaching to use with care

The doctrine of the two kingdoms has had a mixed history. At its best it protects both church and state: the church from becoming a political party, the state from claiming to rule consciences. It honours the ordinary work of government as a service of God. But at its worst it has been read as a reason for Christians to leave politics to rulers and keep their faith private, to obey the state without question, and to say nothing about injustice. Some historians have argued that this helped leave many German Christians passive in the face of later tyranny. Yet others in the same Lutheran tradition, such as Dietrich Bonhoeffer, drew from it the conviction that when the state abandons its God-given task, the church must speak and act.

Luther himself was not consistent. He denied the ruler’s right over conscience, yet leaned on the princes to order the churches. He rebuked tyrants, yet in 1525 sided with them against the poor with a violence that cannot be excused. The reader should take from him the true distinction between the two ways God rules, and take from Scripture the fuller word that rulers are servants of justice, answerable to God for how they treat the weak.

But let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream. AMOS 5:24
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Pray this week for those in government — local and national — by name, that they may restrain evil and protect the weak.

2. Ask whether you have confused the two kingdoms: expecting the state to do the church’s work, or the church to win by worldly power.

3. Name one injustice in your community that grieves you. Consider what faithful, lawful action you could take for your neighbour’s sake.

4. Read Luther’s words in the Peasants’ War as a warning. Examine the way you speak of people on the other side of political divides.

5. If your job involves authority over others, offer it to God as a calling to serve and protect.

A PRAYER
King of kings, You rule the hearts of Your people by Your Word, and You rule the nations by Your providence.
Grant to those in authority wisdom to restrain evil and justice to protect the weak.
Keep Your church from seeking worldly power, and from silence in the face of wrong.
Forgive us when our words are cruel; and let judgment run down as waters, and righteousness as a mighty stream, through Jesus Christ, whose kingdom is not of this world. Amen.

fields.title: The Old Evil Foe
fields.body_html:
Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour: whom resist stedfast in the faith. 1 PETER 5:8–9

Modern readers are often embarrassed by how much Luther talks about the devil. He sees him everywhere: in his own temptations and illnesses, in the storms of history, in the papacy, in the fanatics, in every attack on the gospel. There is a famous story that at the Wartburg he threw his inkpot at the devil, and visitors were long shown a stain on the wall to prove it; the story is almost certainly a legend, and the stain was renewed more than once. But the reality behind the legend is not in doubt. Luther believed that the Christian life is a battle against a real enemy, personal, clever and malicious, who hates Christ and His people. That conviction runs through his hymns, his sermons, his letters and his prayers.

A real enemy

Luther took the Bible’s language about Satan at face value. The devil is the accuser, the liar, the tempter, the murderer from the beginning. He is not a symbol for human wickedness, though he works through it. And his chief target, Luther believed, is not our morality but our faith. The devil does not mind if we are respectable, so long as we trust in ourselves rather than in Christ. His Christmas sermon puts it simply: “the evil spirit attacks nothing so severely as our faith.” And his sermon on the appearing of the grace of God agrees: “The evil spirit will assail only our faith, well knowing that upon it depends all.”

For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against spiritual wickedness in high places. EPHESIANS 6:12

This is why Luther’s own worst temptations were not to gross sin but to despair. The devil would come to him, he said, with the law in his hand, reminding him of his sins, telling him that God was angry, that he had led thousands astray, that he was damned. The accuser does not always lie about our sins. He lies about God’s mercy.

For the accuser of our brethren is cast down, which accused them before our God day and night. And they overcame him by the blood of the Lamb, and by the word of their testimony. REVELATION 12:10–11

The enemy within

Yet Luther was clear that we cannot blame the devil for everything. In his sermon on the appearing of grace, he mocks the idea that we can escape temptation by fleeing into the desert, putting on a monk’s habit, or changing our diet. If our sins were painted on the wall, he says, we could run out of the house; but they are in our own hearts. Then he says, directly:

“Dear man, the great temptations are within you.”

But every man is tempted, when he is drawn away of his own lust, and enticed. JAMES 1:14

The devil works with what he finds in us. That is why the battle cannot be won by outward means alone. It must be fought where the enemy has his foothold: in the heart, by faith.

The weapons of the fight

How then do we fight? Luther’s answer was always the same: with the Word of God. The Christmas sermon, after its long meditation on the birth of Christ, ends with a section on the armour of the Gospel, explaining why it is important to know where each article of faith is found in Scripture. In time of temptation, he says, we must point to that Word, “for the evil spirit can not stand against God’s Word.”

Put on the whole armour of God, that ye may be able to stand against the wiles of the devil. EPHESIANS 6:11
Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked. And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. EPHESIANS 6:16–17

Christ Himself fought that way in the wilderness, answering every temptation with It is written. Luther urged believers to do the same: not to argue with the devil in their own strength, not to debate their feelings, but to answer him with Scripture, with the Creed, with the words I am baptised, with a hymn.

He also recommended scorn. The proud spirit, he said, cannot bear to be despised. Rather than trembling before the devil, the Christian may laugh at him, because he is a defeated enemy.

A defeated foe

That, finally, is the centre of Luther’s teaching on the devil. The enemy is real, but he is beaten. At the cross and the empty tomb, Christ crushed the serpent’s head, as God had promised in the garden. Luther’s Easter sermon rejoices in this victory. Because Christ has taken our sins and risen, the believer can say:

“Now I can defy death, the devil, sin and hell to do me any harm.”

And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel. GENESIS 3:15
And having spoiled principalities and powers, he made a shew of them openly, triumphing over them in it. COLOSSIANS 2:15

This is the note A mighty fortress strikes: the old evil foe is fierce and cunning, and no earthly power can match him; yet a single little word of God can bring him down. The Christian fights, but the Christian fights from victory, not towards it.

Honest cautions

Luther’s vivid sense of the devil had a dark side. Because he saw Satan behind every opposition to the gospel, he was quick to call his opponents the devil’s servants — the pope, Zwingli, the Anabaptists, the rebellious peasants, and in the end the Jews. Once an opponent is simply the devil’s tool, there is little room left for charity, patience or the possibility that one might be wrong. Much of the violence of his polemic grew from this root.

He also shared his age’s belief in witchcraft, and approved the harsh punishment of those accused of it. Here he was a man of his time rather than a teacher to follow. Scripture is sober about the devil. It warns us of his wiles, but it never tells us to see his face in every person who disagrees with us. Our battle is not against flesh and blood.

Submit yourselves therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you. JAMES 4:7
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Where does the accuser most often attack your faith? Find one Scripture that answers that accusation and learn it by heart.

2. Practise Luther’s counsel: when tempted to despair, do not argue with your feelings; answer with the Creed or a verse.

3. Examine your heart for the temptations within you, and confess them rather than blaming circumstances.

4. Consider whether you have demonised someone you disagree with. Pray for them by name as a person, not an enemy.

5. Sing or read A mighty fortress this week as a declaration of Christ’s victory.

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, You have crushed the serpent’s head and triumphed over every power of darkness.
When the accuser speaks, let me answer with Your Word and point to Your cross.
Search out the temptations that lie within my own heart, and give me grace to resist them.
Keep me from seeing enemies where You see souls for whom You died, and let me stand firm, from victory, until the day You bring every enemy under Your feet. Amen.

fields.title: Righteous and a Sinner at Once

There is therefore now no condemnation to them which are in Christ Jesus, who walk not after the flesh, but after the Spirit. ROMANS 8:1

The first of Luther’s ninety-five theses is not about indulgences at all. When our Lord and Master Jesus Christ said, Repent, Luther wrote in effect, He meant the whole life of believers to be one of repentance. It is a quiet sentence, easy to pass over. But it contains a conviction that runs through all his teaching and that he summed up, in his Latin lectures, in a short and startling phrase: simul iustus et peccator. The Christian is at the same time righteous and a sinner.

Two things true at once

What did he mean? Not that the Christian is half righteous and half sinful, as though the two were mixed in a jar and grace were slowly increasing its share. He meant that each is wholly true, from a different point of view. In Christ, before God, the believer is wholly righteous, clothed with Christ’s perfect righteousness, forgiven and accepted. In himself, in his own nature, he is still a sinner, with a heart that remains bent, desires that remain disordered, and a daily need of forgiveness.

If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us. If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness. 1 JOHN 1:8–9

Luther came to this partly through wrestling with the seventh chapter of Romans in his lectures of 1515 and 1516. He became convinced that Paul’s cry — the good that I would I do not — was not the voice of an unbeliever, but of the mature apostle himself, describing the Christian’s lifelong conflict between the Spirit and the flesh.

For the good that I would I do not: but the evil which I would not, that I do. ROMANS 7:19
For the flesh lusteth against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh: and these are contrary the one to the other. GALATIANS 5:17

Still sinners, already healed

Luther’s sermons return to this again and again, often with homely illustrations. In his Pentecost sermon he warns against thinking that anyone who has received the Holy Spirit must be perfect and strong, and says that the Spirit has begun His work but not finished it. Then he offers a picture:

“Our case must be like that of a sick man who is in the hands of the physician; presently he will be better.”

The sick man is truly ill, and truly under the physician’s care; the cure has begun, and it is certain, but it is not yet complete. So with the Christian. He is not yet well. But he is in good hands.

His Easter sermon is blunter. Asking why, if Christ has conquered sin, believers still feel sin stirring in them, Luther answers with a farmyard image that his first hearers would never forget:

“You may tie a hog ever so well, but you cannot prevent it from grunting.”

The old nature is bound and doomed, but it still makes itself heard. Only death, he says, will finally silence it; until then no one is a finished Christian. In the meantime, the sins that remain serve to drive us back to faith, so that faith may grow from day to day.

O wretched man that I am! who shall deliver me from the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ our Lord. ROMANS 7:24–25

Growth is real

This does not mean that Luther thought the Christian stands still. The same Easter sermon compares the work of grace to leaven hidden in the dough, which must slowly work through the whole lump until everything is leavened. And his sermon on the appearing of the grace of God says that although faith frees at once from all guilt, evil desires cling to body and soul like the smell and sickness of a dungeon, and must be purged. He concludes:

“Until death our lives should be nothing but purification.”

He compares it to Lazarus, raised by a single word, yet still needing the grave-clothes unwound; and to the wounded man in the parable, rescued by the Samaritan yet left in the inn to be nursed back to health. Justification is complete; sanctification is a lifelong recovery.

Not as though I had already attained, either were already perfect: but I follow after, if that I may apprehend that for which also I am apprehended of Christ Jesus. PHILIPPIANS 3:12
Being confident of this very thing, that he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ. PHILIPPIANS 1:6

Why it matters

This teaching brings enormous freedom. It frees the Christian from despair when he discovers, yet again, how much sin remains in him. Such discoveries do not mean he is not a Christian; they mean he is a Christian in the middle of the cure. It frees him from pretending, from the exhausting effort to appear more holy than he is. And it frees him from judging others harshly, since he knows that he too is a sinner saved only by grace.

It also explains Luther himself. He could write the gentlest pages on grace and the harshest pages against his enemies; he could comfort the dying and curse the peasants. We should not excuse his sins because of his teaching. But his teaching helps us understand how a man truly justified by faith could still sin so grievously, and it warns every one of us that the same is possible in our own lives.

An honest caution

Like every truth, this one can be misused. If the Christian is always a sinner, he may be tempted to shrug at his sin and make no effort to change: I am simul iustus et peccator, so what can you expect? That is not Luther’s teaching. He never said that sin does not matter, only that it does not condemn. Later traditions, especially those that followed John Wesley, pressed harder than Luther on the hope of real victory over sin in this life, and they were right to guard against complacency. Luther’s own words about lifelong purification show that he would agree. The right response to remaining sin is neither despair nor indifference, but repentance, faith and the daily fight.

And the publican, standing afar off, would not lift up so much as his eyes unto heaven, but smote upon his breast, saying, God be merciful to me a sinner. LUKE 18:13
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. When you next discover sin in yourself that you thought was gone, do not despair. Confess it, and say, “I am still in the Physician’s hands.”

2. Read Romans 7:14–8:4 in one sitting, and notice how the cry of chapter 7 leads into the freedom of chapter 8.

3. Name one area where you have excused sin on the grounds that everyone is a sinner. Take one concrete step against it this week.

4. Consider someone whose faults irritate you. Remember that you are both sinners in the process of being healed, and pray for them.

5. Begin each day this week with the publican’s prayer, and end it with Romans 8:1.

A PRAYER
Merciful Father, in Christ You count me righteous, and in myself I am still a sinner.
Thank You that there is no condemnation for those who are in Him, and that my standing with You does not rise and fall with my progress.
Keep me from despair when I find sin in me, and from indifference when I would excuse it.
Finish the good work You have begun, until the day when the old self is silenced for ever and I am wholly Yours. Amen.

fields.title: In the Midst of Dying Is Life
fields.body_html:
O death, where is thy sting? O grave, where is thy victory? The sting of death is sin; and the strength of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, which giveth us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ. 1 CORINTHIANS 15:55–57

Luther lived close to death. Plague came to Wittenberg more than once. He lost two daughters, his parents, many friends and colleagues. He was often ill and several times thought himself dying. He was an outlaw under sentence of death for the last twenty-five years of his life. And the fear of death and judgement had driven him into the monastery in the first place. It is no surprise, then, that some of his most tender and practical writing is for the dying and those who care for them. The man who began his Christian life terrified of death ended it, by all accounts, at peace.

Looking at death in Christ

In 1519, at the request of a friend, Luther wrote a short Sermon on Preparing to Die. It is one of his most pastoral works, and its counsel is simple. When we are dying, he says in effect, we are assailed by three terrible pictures: death itself, our sins, and the fear of hell. The devil loves to hold these before our eyes. We must not stare at them. Instead, we should look at each of them in Christ. Look at death not in itself, but in Christ, who has overcome it. Look at sin not in yourself, but in Christ, who bore it away. Look at hell not in yourself, but in Christ, who suffered it for you and rose again. We should not dwell on these things during our dying, but look to the picture of Christ crucified and risen.

Who shall lay any thing to the charge of God’s elect? It is God that justifieth. Who is he that condemneth? It is Christ that died, yea rather, that is risen again. ROMANS 8:33–34

Luther’s sermon on the appearing of the grace of God makes the same argument about the day of judgement. The judge on that day, he says, will be Christ, who gave Himself for our sins. How can He condemn those for whom He died? He would first have to deny His own sacrifice:

“He would have to condemn himself before sin could condemn the souls for whom he died.”

For me

The heart of Luther’s comfort is, again, the two small words for me. It is not enough, he says in his Easter sermon, to know that Christ died and rose, as a fact of history. What makes the heart rejoice is to know that all of it was done for me. Then, he says, “when I come to understand the fact that all the works God does in Christ are done for me … the effect of his resurrection being that I also will arise and live with him; that will cause me to rejoice.”

Who was delivered for our offences, and was raised again for our justification. ROMANS 4:25
Jesus said unto her, I am the resurrection, and the life: he that believeth in me, though he were dead, yet shall he live: and whosoever liveth and believeth in me shall never die. JOHN 11:25–26

Life in the midst of death

A well-known medieval chant began, In the midst of life we are in death. Luther turned it into a German hymn, and in his preaching he loved to turn it around. The gospel says the opposite: in the midst of death we are in life. His Pentecost sermon, speaking of the peace the Holy Spirit gives, puts it in words that could be written over every Christian deathbed:

“Thus, in the midst of dying is life; and in the midst of trouble, peace and joy.”

And a little later in the same sermon he imagines Christ speaking to the fearful believer: “just pass down into the valley of death; there shall the Holy Spirit come to you and make you so courageous and joyful that you will not know death, yea, it will be sweet to you.”

Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me; thy rod and thy staff they comfort me. PSALM 23:4

Honest about fear

Luther did not pretend that Christians never fear death. The same Pentecost sermon warns believers not to conclude that the Spirit has left them because they still shudder at it. Faith grows by degrees, and the Spirit comforts precisely those who are afraid. Luther himself confessed his fear of death many times. He was not a stoic. He knew that death is an enemy, the last enemy, and that it is right to grieve.

And deliver them who through fear of death were all their lifetime subject to bondage. HEBREWS 2:15

In 1527, when plague struck Wittenberg, he was asked whether a Christian may flee a deadly plague. His answer, in a letter later printed, was balanced and wise. Those with duties to the sick — pastors, officials, doctors, neighbours with no one else to care for them — should stay and serve. Others may leave without sin, for it is not wrong to preserve one’s life, and to rush into danger without need is to tempt God. He urged sensible precautions: cleansing the air, taking medicine, avoiding needless contact. Faith does not despise ordinary means. He and Katharina stayed, and nursed the sick in their home.

Beggars at the last

When his own father lay dying in 1530, Luther, unable to travel because he was an outlaw, wrote him a letter of comfort, urging him to cling to Christ and to see death as a sleep. When his daughter Magdalena died, he wept and gave her back to God. And when his own death came at Eisleben in 1546, he commended his spirit to God in the words of the Psalm, and answered his friend’s question with a clear yes: he died trusting the Christ he had preached. The note found beside him said that we are beggars, and that this is true. It is the right last word for a theologian of grace. At the end, no one comes to God with anything in his hands.

Blessed are the poor in spirit: for theirs is the kingdom of heaven. MATTHEW 5:3
Lord, now lettest thou thy servant depart in peace, according to thy word: for mine eyes have seen thy salvation. LUKE 2:29–30
FOR REFLECTION AND ACTION

1. Think honestly about your own death. Pray Psalm 90:12, asking God to teach you to number your days.

2. When you think of death, practise Luther’s counsel: look not at death, your sins or judgement in themselves, but at each of them in Christ.

3. If someone you know is dying, visit them. Read them a promise such as John 11:25–26, and pray with them simply.

4. If you are afraid of death, do not be ashamed. Tell God so, and ask for the Spirit’s comfort in your fear.

5. Write a short statement of faith that you would want read at your funeral, beginning with the words: “I am a beggar, made rich in Christ.”

A PRAYER
Lord Jesus Christ, You tasted death for me and rose again, and You hold the keys of death and of the grave.
When my time comes, let me look not at death, nor at my sins, nor at judgement, but at You, crucified and risen for me.
Comfort me in my fear, and give me the peace that is life in the midst of dying.
Receive me at the last as a beggar made rich by Your grace, and raise me up to live with You for ever. Amen.

fields.title: Conclusion
fields.body_html:
For of him, and through him, and to him, are all things: to whom be glory for ever. Amen. ROMANS 11:36

Twenty chapters may give the impression that Luther taught many things. He did write on almost everything — on the Bible and the sacraments, on marriage and money, on schools and princes, on music and plague. But at the centre of it all is one discovery, made by a frightened friar over the letter to the Romans: the righteousness that God requires is the righteousness God gives. Everything else he taught is that discovery followed out into the whole of life.

Follow the thread and the shape appears. God’s righteousness is a gift, received by faith alone, and faith is the heart’s trust that Christ is for me. God is found not where we look for Him in glory, but hidden in the cross. The law shows us our sin; the gospel gives us Christ. Faith makes the Christian lord of all, and love makes him servant of all. The will cannot free itself; only God can turn it, and He does so by His Word. That Word gives every believer access to God and makes every believer a priest for others. It turns ordinary work into holy calling. It comes to us in water, bread and wine, with the promise for you. We answer it in prayer, learn it in the catechism, sing it in hymns, and cling to it in the dark, when the old enemy accuses and our feelings fail. We remain sinners to the end, yet righteous in Christ; and at the end we come to Him as beggars, and find life in the midst of dying.

What he got wrong

This book has not hidden Luther’s sins, and it would be a false tribute to end by doing so. Some of them were the ordinary faults of a passionate and overworked man — impatience, pride, a temper that flared. Others were public and grave.

The gravest was his writing against the Jews. In his early years he had rebuked Christians for their cruelty to Jewish people, and in 1523 he wrote a treatise reminding his readers that Jesus Christ was born a Jew. His sermon on Christ’s sufferings, in this library, begins by warning against those who meditate on the passion only to rage at Judas and the Jews. But when the Jews did not turn to the gospel as he had hoped, he turned on them. In 1543, three years before his death, he published On the Jews and Their Lies and other writings urging that synagogues and schools be burned, Jewish homes destroyed, their books taken, their rabbis silenced, and their people driven out or set to forced labour. There is no way to soften this. It was a betrayal of the gospel he preached and of the Jewish Christ he worshipped. These writings were revived by antisemites in later centuries and used by the Nazis to lend Luther’s name to their hatred, in a century when six million Jews were murdered. Many Lutheran churches have since formally repudiated them, and every reader of Luther must do the same.

He also called for the slaughter of the rebel peasants in 1525; approved the death penalty for Anabaptists; secretly counselled a prince to commit bigamy; poured coarse and abusive language on popes, fellow Reformers and opponents; and refused fellowship to Christians who differed from him over the Lord’s Supper. These were not small failings. They caused real suffering, and some of them helped to harden the divisions of the church for centuries.

Search me, O God, and know my heart: try me, and know my thoughts: and see if there be any wicked way in me, and lead me in the way everlasting. PSALM 139:23–24

None of this is raised to cancel what he saw. It is raised because his own teaching demands it. Luther taught that the justified believer is still a sinner, that even the best teachers can err, and that everything must be tested by the Word of God. He would not want his sins excused for the sake of his doctrine. He would want his doctrine to be judged by Scripture, and his sins to be named as sins. The honest reader will hold both: gratitude for the gospel he recovered, and grief for the harm he did.

What to carry away

If you carry nothing else from this book, carry three things.

First, the two words for you. The gospel is not a report about other people. Christ was born, died and rose for you. Faith is taking it personally.

Second, the difference between feeling and faith. Your standing with God does not rise and fall with your emotions or your progress. It rests on Christ and His promise. When your feelings fail, go back to the Word, to your baptism, to the table, to the cross.

Third, the freedom that makes us servants. Because you are already accepted, you do not have to earn anything. So you are free to spend your life on your neighbour — in your family, your work, your community — as Christ spent His on you.
